news.title: Manchester City v Paris Saint-Germain: Champions League – live
news.desc: Champions League news from the 8pm BST kick-off Live scoreboard | Today’s Football Daily | Email Scott 2 min: Cherki is caught dozing by Dembélé, who sends Doué scampering down a cul-de-sac on the left. Cherki will be pleased Khusanov was on point there. PSG, in their blue shirts with red central panel, launch the kick-off in their usual rugby-union style. City in their sky blue. Continue reading...
text: Not sure how there were only (!) six (!!) goals in the end. That could have ended 2-10, 6-6, 8-6 or anything in between. Manchester City were much improved in the second half, but paid the price for not turning up for the first, during which PSG at times went into full Harlem Globetrotters mode. The reigning champions were outrageously good; the half-time scoreline of 0-3 didn’t flatter them at all. City will take succour from the performances of two-goal Erling Haaland, plus the second-half subs Iliman Ndiaye and Ayyoub Bouaddi, but on this evidence PSG are going to take some stopping, especially if they can keep their concentration for the full 90. Very early doors, of course, but the three-peat looks very much on for Luis Enrique’s side, who celebrate with feeling in front of their fans.
Luis Enrique and Enzo Maresca embrace. Their teams put on one hell of a show.

90 min +3: Kvaratskhelia hasn’t done much since coming on. Not by his lofty standards. He tries to address that with a power-dribble down the middle, then a probe down the right, but there’s nothing doing.

90 min: … and after a stop and skip, Torres scuffs towards the bottom right. Easy for Donnarumma! The City fans enjoyed that. Then Fernandez makes way for O’Reilly. There will be four additional minutes.
89 min: … but Nunes had made the slightest of contact. Torres to take. Loud boos for the former City man as he prepares to take …
87 min: PSG clear and counter. Mendes and Torres one-two down the middle. Mendes enters the box, only to be nicked by Nunes. The referee points to the spot.

86 min: Haaland rolls a pass into the PSG box from the left. Semenyo bustles. He can’t get a shot away, not at first, but eventually slices over from ten yards. Big miss. Or did that take a nick? It took a nick. Corner. From which …
84 min: A PSG double-switch as Hernandez and Beraldo replace Ruiz and Zaire-Emery.

83 min: Nunes races into the PSG box down the right and crosses low for Haaland, who slides in at the far stick and hook-forces the ball goalwards … only for Safonov to sensationally block on the line. Wonderful play all around.
82 min: Luis Enrique comes to the touchline and gives his players some beneficial advice, utilising letters such as F and JEFF.
80 min: Semenyo threads a long-range drive towards the bottom right. Easy for Safonov.
78 min: Neves nearly releases Torres down the inside-left channel with a mid-pirouette side-footed volley. Not quite, because Khusanov slides in to flick clear. That would have been some assist.

77 min: Hakimi has the chance to release Torres down the middle, but looks for Kvaratskhelia on the left instead. Bad decision. Kvaratskhelia enters the box and drags a tame shot across Donnarumma and wide right.
76 min: PSG respond by replacing Dembélé and Akliouche with João Neves and former City striker Ferran Torres.
Bouaddi one-twos his way down the right and cuts back for Haaland, who sweeps into the bottom left from 12 yards. It’s on! Again! Maybe!

74 min: The referee Sven Jablonski is shoved over from behind by Fernandez. Hilarity ensues. While that’s going on, Gvardiol crosses from the left. Haaland wins a header at the far stick and pings the ball off the top of the crossbar. But no matter, because …

72 min: Anderson drives in from the left and shoots from distance. It’s deflected over for another City corner. Fernandez’s delivery isn’t so good this time, but PSG fail to clear their lines, and the ball drops to Semenyo, whose low shot is blocked by Pacho. Then the flag pops up for offside.
71 min: … and now Fernandez pings a long-range shot off the junction of right-hand post and crossbar. This game is proper daft.
70 min: Fernandez takes what is effectively a corner from the left. Gvardiol flicks a header towards the top right. It’s heading in, but Mendes eyebrows off the line and clear!

69 min: Anderson jinks his way past Zaire-Emery near the left-hand corner flag. He’s scuttling clear along the byline when he’s cynically brought down by the man he’s just beaten. Zaire-Emery goes into the book.
68 min: Fernandez slips Haaland into a bit of space down the left. Haaland slices wildly over the bar in a state of great irritation.
66 min: If this isn’t bad enough for City, here comes the best winger in the world, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. He replaces Désiré Doué.

65 min: That goal has taken all of the air out of the stadium … and from Manchester City’s sail. Semenyo tries to whip up the storm again, nipping past Pacho on the right before rippling the side netting. Safonov had it covered.
64 min: Haaland tries to hit back immediately, but his thunderous shot from an angle on the right sails harmlessly wide left.

On the edge of the City D, Akliouche picks up Dembele’s low pass from the right, his back to goal. He takes a touch, turns, and peals a shot towards the top left. Donnarumma gets a strong hand to stop it going in … but not strong enough, because when the ball drops back down and lands, the spin takes it back towards the net and over the line.
62 min: Haaland has reached the 37-goal mark in 60 Champions League matches; for the record, it took Lionel Messi 80.
60 min: Semenyo feeds Nunes on the overlap down the right. Nunes crosses long for Ndiaye, who shins his shot from eight yards. Now it’s PSG’s turn to look a bit ragged.

58 min: Fernandez crosses long from the left. Haaland flicks on. The ball sails wide right, but any touch from either Guehi or Khusanov, both sliding in, would have surely cut the deficit in half. City have been fantastic since the break.
57 min: Ndiaye has been an electric eel since coming on at the break. He sizzles his way down the left again, trying to force home from a tight angle. Safonov does just enough.
56 min: Haaland is now Manchester City’s number-one goalscorer in Champions League history, by the way. His 37th in the competition for the club puts him one ahead of Sergio Agüero.

55 min: Semenyo jigs in from the left, seeing Pacho off with ease, only to lift his shot over Safonov and off the crossbar. The ball drops to Haaland, who air-whiffs his shot from eight yards! How on earth did he not score?! But his blushes are spared, because turns out Semenyo was offside at the start of the move anyway.
54 min: That’s got the crowd going for the first time tonight. And how! And then …

Mendes really should be booked for wrapping his arms around Semenyo’s waist. But somehow no. Then from the free kick, Ndiaye nearly forces a low shot into the bottom left, only for Safonov to parry. But then he picks up possession again, swinging in from the left. Haaland power-glances a header across Safonov and into the top right! Is it on?
51 min: A PSG free kick near the centre circle. Nuno Mendes goes for goal, having spotted Donnarumma off his line. Not quite, but full marks for sass and ambition.

49 min: Semenyo dribbles artfully down the right and curls a cross towards Fernandez at the far stick. Fernandez has to convert this sensational cross … but slaps a downward header wide left. City should be on the scoresheet, and speaking of which, here’s Matt Dony with a quip he describes himself as the “lowest of low-hanging fruit … if City carry on playing this badly, it could end 1-114!”

48 min: Haaland barrels down the left and clips a low pass across to Semenyo, whose drive from the edge of the box is deflected high and wide. Haaland couldn’t get the ball out from under his feet to shoot himself. Anyway, the resulting corner comes to nothing, but City have flown out of the blocks here, clearly having been given the half-time what-for.
46 min: Two of the subs quickly into the action. Bouaddi creams a diagonal towards Ndiaye on the left. Ndiaye cuts into the box before hoicking harmlessly over.
City get the second half started. They’ve made a triple change, hooking Cherki, Doku and Dias for Nunes, Bouaddi and Ndiaye.

Half-time postbag. “That 30-odd minutes of football from PSG is some of the best I’ve ever seen. At this level football transcends sport into something approaching art. Just amazing to watch” – Martin Gamage

“Say what you will about the tenets of the Qatari government, but at least they built a team worth the money. From spending a decade as Europe’s most dependable clown show, they’re now quite possibly the best club side since peak-Messi’s peak-Barcelona” – Walter Sobchak Kári Tulinius

news.title: Bradley Barcola’s clinical hat-trick inspires Liverpool to 6-3 rout of Lask

text: Liverpool cleansed themselves from the stains of defeat by Manchester City at the earliest opportunity. A rampant display in Austria saw Bradley Barcola ignite his Liverpool account with the first hat-trick of his professional career and Andoni Iraola’s team devastate Lask’s big night in the Champions League. The major surprise was how the hosts managed to score three.

Iraola’s pre-match faith in the big-money signings Barcola and Florian Wirtz was repaid as the pair helped dismantle limited opponents. But it was not all about the money and the £123m signing from Paris Saint-Germain scoring the first goals of his Liverpool career. Lewis Koumas registered his first goal in the competition and replaced Steven Gerrard as the youngest player to score and assist in a Champions League game for Liverpool. A total of 26 shots equalled Liverpool’s record in a Champions League away game.

“I’m really happy for Bradley,” said the Liverpool head coach. “Yesterday you were asking me a lot about his numbers, and also Flo [Wirtz], and both of them played really well. They made a difference. Apart from the hat-trick Bradley was a threat one-v-one, helped us control the game and defended the pockets. It will do their confidence good for sure.”

The home end was full and in strong voice over an hour before kick-off as Lask supporters came to savour their club’s first home game in the Champions League proper. The Lask team proved to be much less impressive though, in fairness to the Austrian crowd, their support rarely wavered even as a rout unfolded before their eyes. Liverpool revelled in their superiority and the invitation to recover from Sunday’s first defeat of the season.

Iraola rested Virgil van Dijk, delaying the defender’s 200th game as Liverpool captain, and Alexis Mac Allister as he managed workloads ahead of Saturday’s visit to Brentford. A new-look central defence of Ronald Araújo and Jérémy Jacquet were given a physical test by the Lask strikers Samuel Adeniran and Krystof Danek but handled the host’s rudimental approach comfortably.

Liverpool were utterly dominant against an opponent that struggled to retain possession in all areas of the pitch. The breakthrough was inevitable but also a result of a mix-up in the Lask defence between Alemão and the goalkeeper, Lukas Jungwirth. From the second corner that followed their error, Araújo towered above his marker to head home Kostas Tsimikas’s delivery. It was the Uruguay international’s first Liverpool goal and the start of an onslaught.

Merely 96 seconds later it was 2-0 as Barcola also scored his first Liverpool goal. The summer recruit found himself under scrutiny ahead of the game, along with Wirtz, having gone six appearances for his new club without a goal or an assist. That issue was put to bed when Rio Ngumoha weaved in from the right and Koumas laid the ball back to the lurking winger. Barcola swept a first-time shot inside Jungwirth’s far post. Liverpool were enjoying themselves.

Wirtz soon found himself with a much-needed assist for Barcola’s second goal. The Germany international has looked more at home for Liverpool in the Champions League than Premier League and this was no exception. Wirtz picked out Barcola’s run into the Lask area and the winger rolled a cool finish beyond the exposed keeper.

Lask could have been seriously embarrassed before half-time. Koumas had a fine finish disallowed for offside and, following another neat exchange between Wirtz and Barcola, Ryan Gravenberch’s shot kissed the inside of the far post. Liverpool’s 19 attempts on goal were the most by an away side in the first half of a Champions League game since records began in 2003-04.

There would be no letup from Iraola’s team after the interval. Jeremie Frimpong morphed into an old-fashioned centre-forward to rise above Yvan Dibango and bury a textbook header into the bottom corner from Tsimikas’s cross. Koumas had a second goal disallowed for offside before Alisson’s clean sheet was ruined by the Lask substitute Robert Ljubicic sweeping home inside his near post. Barcola was presented with his hat-trick when Ngumoha released Frimpong and the full-back flashed a low cross through the Lask six-yard box. Barcola applied a simple finish at the back post.

Frimpong also supplied the assist for Koumas’s deserved goal, converted from close range after the home side were caught playing out from the back. The Lask substitute Florian Flecker brought a touch of respectability to the scoreline with two goals in four minutes, both set up by Dibango, but there was no disguising the emphatic manner of Liverpool’s victory nor the surge of confidence it should give to Barcola.

news.title: Kevin Pietersen tells ECB he will not promote gambling site while on England duty
news.desc: Specialist mentor signed lucrative deal with online firm Board’s strict code prohibits betting across cricket Kevin Pietersen has told the England and Wales Cricket Board he will not promote betting while on duty as England’s specialist mentor. text: Kevin Pietersen has told the England and Wales Cricket Board he will not promote betting while on duty as England’s specialist mentor. Pietersen signed a lucrative contract as a brand ambassador for an online gambling company this week.

The former England batter is contracted to work with Brendon McCullum’s white-ball team for around 150 days over the next 13 months until the conclusion of the 50-over World Cup co-hosted by South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia. Pietersen’s betting ­interests create a potential headache for his employers.

The ECB’s anti-corruption code bans participants from “directly or indirectly soliciting, inducing, enticing, instructing, persuading, encouraging, facilitating or authorising any other party to enter into a bet in relation to the result, progress, conduct or any other aspect of any match or competition.”

The ECB does not take advertising revenue from gambling companies, has banned Hundred franchises from sponsorship deals with betting firms from next year and its regulations state that any counties accepting commercial gambling income must demonstrate that the proceeds are reinvested into infrastructure projects or community programmes.

All participants in cricket are also prohibited from betting, a rule that led to the England fast bowler Brydon Carse being given a 16-month ban – 13 of which were suspended – two years ago for placing 303 bets between 2017 and 2019.

Pietersen announced he is joining the Philippines-based Dafabet on Monday. The 46-year-old is understood to have reassured the ECB, however, that he will not promote Dafabet while on England duty, which given the extent of his commitments over the next year will prove restrictive.

While Pietersen is not travelling to Pakistan for a 50-over tri series also featuring Sri Lanka that starts next week, he will play a full part in the winter tours of Australia and South Africa, as well as all England’s domestic white-ball matches next summer leading into the World Cup.

The ECB previously had issues regarding McCullum’s betting interests after the then Test coach joined the Cyprus-based company 22bet as an ambassador three years ago. He went on to promote its Indian Premier League betting markets on Facebook and YouTube.

The ECB concluded that McCullum was not in breach of its anti-corruption code, although he opted to terminate his relationship with 22bet anyway. Unlike 22bet, which is licensed offshore in Curacao, Dafabet has a licence to operate in the UK.

text: Organisations such as 180 Project and Prison Run are helping to prepare prisoners for release with a fresh view on life on the outside

On the day 700 prisoners in England and Wales were released early, I was driving to Wolverhampton for an event organised by the not-for-profit group ConnectSport. It was to celebrate local sports clubs and initiatives that “help young people believe in themselves and realise what they’re capable of” as described by Ranjit Singh, a local legend in the world of wrestling, martial arts and Kabaddi.

I listened to several news cycles that detailed the risks of early release pitched against the intractable challenge of insufficient prison capacity. It was presented as a hopeless logjam with no solutions. Tagging was the only option mentioned as a way of reducing reoffending rates.

There is clearly no single solution, but it is an area where sport can and does make a difference and could do in a greater way, particularly if we start to see sport as more than a source of entertainment or physical fitness.

In his annual report, Charlie Taylor, HM chief inspector of prisons for England and Wales, emphasised the serious need to improve prisoners’ access to gyms and physical activity. Where it works, it works powerfully.

Twenty-five prisons and young offender institutions organise parkrun and research shows a range of benefits, including better mental and physical health; improved self-esteem and confidence; increased sense of purpose and achievement; and the creation of a safe, humanising and non-judgmental space in which to be active, feel valued and respected. All crucial factors that contribute to rehabilitation and reduced reoffending.

The former triathlete Chrissie Wellington, the Ironman world champion, is leading a new initiative, Prison Run, to train 20 men and women from three prisons, all nearing release, to run the 2027 London Marathon. Most will never have run more than a few miles. A group of mentors will coach them from their first run to marathon distance in prison, on temporary release days and post-release. They plan to bolster fitness programmes inside prison and provide support for life outside prison by connecting sport, mentoring, employment and community.

John McAvoy, a Nike-sponsored triathlete who broke world indoor rowing records while in prison for armed robbery, will be part of the coaching team. McAvoy describes Prison Run as a chance to “break the cycle” where 67.1% of adults released from sentences of less than 12 months reoffend.

Sport transformed McEvoy’s life and gave him a purpose, a community and a burning belief that the past does not have to define the future. He is driven to share it with others. “Everyone deserves a second chance,” he says. “Sometimes they just need someone to believe in them and I will as I run alongside them during this special event.”

Sport and physical activity can contribute to the much-needed pathway “through the gate” that is so broken. Highly praised by Taylor, 180 Project engages prisoners in CrossFit and connects them to a community when they come out with housing, life-coaching and other vital support services linked around the gym.

The project leaders invited me to run an indoor rowing masterclass. I met a group of motivated prisoners in their last year or so behind bars, hungry for tips to improve their scores and know what 500m splits to aim for on the rowing machine. Most crucially, they were building a new, common language, positive behaviours and a fresh perspective on life and community that could lead to a different future path.

One of the prisoners who left four months ago had been in and out of prison from the age of 15 and found more than fitness through 180 Project. He describes becoming part of a community and family of people “all dealing with something” and credits this project with “building my own self-awareness, becoming a better person to see the potential that’s inside”.
Lindsey Middleton, the inspiration co-founder of 180 Project, told me “people get physically, mentally, emotionally well and socially connected” through what they do.

It is an area where the UK has been building world-leading expertise. The Alliance of Sport in Criminal Justice connects local sports organisations with academics and government partners for a clearer understanding of how sport can help reduce crime.

Under James Mapstone’s leadership the alliance has gained a global reputation leading to a request to produce a youth crime prevention initiative across south-east Asia for the International Olympic Committee, funded by the French Development Agency.

The project aims to support 82,000 young people through 11 projects in Laos, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam. Across the region, sport is being taken seriously as a tool to prevent youth crime and strengthen community resilience.
This work has been a priority for Kirsty Coventry since she became the IOC president and chose to emphasise sport’s role in fostering safer and stronger communities.

A recent poll from Forward Trust, a charity that supports people to recover from addiction and leave crime behind, showed strong public support for the use of rehabilitation programmes. The current crisis offers a moment where sport and physical activity could contribute to that on a bigger scale through its ability to influence communities, shape identities, work with government and other public authorities while adapting to local needs.

These ideas aren’t new. Prof Rosie Meek, a chartered psychologist and prison scholar at Royal Holloway, University of London has been researching the positive effect of sport and physical activity in prisons for more than 20 years.

Yet it remains underutilised. The role of sport and physical activity within prison life is overdue an update in order to understand the broader developmental and social benefits beyond physical fitness.

Outside, there is great scope to develop sport’s contributions to social challenges across our communities. Wellington has pledged through Prison Run to use sport to replace stigma with real stories of resilience, potential and second chances. Imagine a world where that becomes a proud part of sport’s contribution to the country.

news.title: ‘I expect more’: the key questions from Martínez’s Manchester United broadside | Jamie Jackson
news.desc: From Jason Wilcox’s role to the views of the rest of the squad, we tackle the major talking points at Old Trafford after the defender’s outburst After Manchester United’s 2-0 loss at Atlético Madrid, Lisandro Martínez teed off at the director of football, Jason Wilcox, and the rest of the executive. “We don’t have the best squad at the moment compared with other top teams,” said the defender. “I expect more [investment], 100%. text: From Jason Wilcox’s role to the views of the rest of the squad, we tackle the major talking points at Old Trafford after the defender’s outburst

After Manchester United’s 2-0 loss at Atlético Madrid, Lisandro Martínez teed off at the director of football, Jason Wilcox, and the rest of the executive. “We don’t have the best squad at the moment compared with other top teams,” said the defender. “I expect more [investment], 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox] … Really poor [the Atlético defeat] – I have to control myself a lot but something is a reflection of the mirror of how our club is at the moment.” Here we consider the key questions emerging from Martínez’s explosive remarks.

Yes is the short answer. The Guardian has been told the decision to target three midfielders in Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans and Carlos Baleba caused bemusement in the squad that no other areas were strengthened in the summer. Carrick led United to third last term after the side only had 17 league games remaining when he took over in January, having been eliminated from the other competitions. The need for defensive reinforcements is particularly acute because the back four of Diogo Dalot, Martínez, Harry Maguire and Luke Shaw has been together since 2022. Martínez is out of contract next summer and it is thought the 28-year-old may not be offered a new deal or have his one-year option triggered by the club, so teammates are conscious his outburst also came because he expects to leave.

As United’s director of football the 55-year-old wields near-unilateral power on football decisions, with only Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who controls sporting policy, above him. If the buck stops with the executive, the most recent transfer window was Wilcox’s responsibility. This was the latest in a line of missteps on his United record. One concerns when Dan Ashworth (Wilcox’s predecessor) was on gardening leave from Newcastle in the first half of 2024, Wilcox interviewed potential replacements for Erik ten Hag before, oddly, deeming that the head coach should stay. The Dutchman signed a fresh contract but was sacked that autumn. Another involves Wilcox’s major falling out with the man he hired as the Dutchman’s successor, Ruben Amorim, after which the Portuguese said the director of football had told him he should change his favoured 3-4-3 shape. “I came here to be the manager of Manchester United – not to be the coach of Manchester United,” said Amorim, after a 1-1 draw at Leeds on 4 January (his job title was head coach). He was sacked the next day. Wilcox worked with Omar Berrada, United’s chief executive, at Manchester City, where Berrada rose to become chief football operations officer, and Wilcox became academy director. Wilcox moved to Southampton and became director of football from summer 2023 until April 2024, when he joined United, having been identified by Berrada, so there is scrutiny of his experience at elite level.

The 45-year-old’s ability to prosper is related to the quality of Wilcox’s work, primarily in the market, so he cannot be solely responsible for a dire six points from six league games and two victories in all competitions all season. Yet by definition his role as head coach demands Carrick do the best with his resources, and that progress is made on the training ground. On matchdays there is scant excuse for United’s disjointedness, inferior running stats and inability, twice, to take advantage against 10 men: the 1-0 loss to City and Saturday’s 1-1 draw with Tottenham. How is Carrick viewed by his players? According to Santos they back him. “We believe in the manager, we believe in the whole staff, we believe in [ourselves as] players,” he said after the Atlético game. “We are in a bad moment but we have to work to change this result.”.

For further evidence see Amad Diallo’s Snapchat post after the defeat by Atlético: “Fucking disgrace; I have no words.” So United have a World Cup-winner, Martínez, aiming shots at Wilcox and by implication Ratcliffe and Berrada, and a fellow senior player, Diallo, cursing but in ambiguous fashion, adding to the sense of meltdown at the club because it is unclear whether the “disgrace” meant the performance, Martínez’s diatribe, the squad his teammate referred to as not good enough, or something else. All of this is mirrored on the pitch, where United’s 671.4km run in the Premier League is the fifth-lowest (Arsenal’s 716.2 is the highest), and their 581 sprints the fourth-lowest (Brentford’s 765 the most).

In mitigation Wilcox can point to the six American siblings, who remain majority owners and whose family has placed an eye-watering £1.1bn-plus debt on the club that severely restricts the transfer budget. Wilcox oversaw a £155m summer outlay and a net spend of about £100m in a summer when City’s corresponding figures were £457.5m and about £175m. City buying players such as Enzo Fernández (for a British record-equalling £125m), Elliot Anderson (£115m), Ayyoub Bouaddi (£81m) and Iliman Ndiaye (£65m) showed their greater financial muscle, helped by being much better sellers of talent. How they have reached this point has, though, been thrown into sharp focus by last month’s verdict that they have serially cheated.

Any straw should be clutched at so Carrick and his staff can view the first 97 minutes of Baleba’s United career as a rosy augury. After entering on 59 minutes against Spurs, a cute swivel and deft chip to Bruno Fernandes was a moment as impressive as the rest of his debut, and at Atlético the 22-year-old hunted down opponents and crunched into tackles, suggesting his game contains energy, muscularity and skill. It’s early days but perhaps if Baleba had been fit to start the campaign (he was recovering from an ankle problem) he might have affected one or more of the defeat at Hull, the 2-2 draw at Everton when Ainsley Maitland-Niles equalised late, the 1-0 loss to City when Phil Foden was sent off after 23 minutes or the Carabao Cup elimination by Brighton.

news.title: Gianni Infantino faces grilling at potentially ‘explosive’ Fifa council meeting
news.desc: World Cup sell-off, Balogun and peace prize on agenda Opponents will press home need for independent review Gianni Infantino will be questioned by Fifa council members over his involvement in the aborted World Cup sell-off plan , the Folarin Balogun affair and the decision to award Donald Trump the inaugural Fifa peace prize at what is expected to be a heated meeting at the world governing body’s headquarters on Thursday. text: Gianni Infantino will be questioned by Fifa council members over his involvement in the aborted World Cup sell-off plan, the Folarin Balogun affair and the decision to award Donald Trump the inaugural Fifa peace prize at what is expected to be a heated meeting at the world governing body’s headquarters on Thursday.

The Fifa president rejected repeated calls for an extraordinary general meeting of council in the summer after the emergence of the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposals, but will meet his critics for the first time since then in Zurich, with one attender predicting that the talks could be “explosive”.

Aleksander Ceferin, Victor Montagliani and Sheikh Salman Bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, the presidents of Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation respectively, all of whom have called for Infantino to resign, will be present to press home demands for an independent review of Fifa’s governance.

In response to letters from Ceferin, Montagliani and Salman sent last month Infantino pledged to commission an external review of Fifa’s future governance, but no details have been forthcoming, and there is scepticism over whether it will be truly independent.

In addition to FFE, Balogun and the peace prize, which featured on an agenda circulated by Fifa last month, Infantino is also likely to face questions about a report in the Times this week that he received a “second salary” of about £1.3m in 2024, on top of the £3.9m declared in Fifa’s accounts.

US Internal Revenue Service filings show a Fifa subsidiary in charge of running last summer’s World Cup paid Infantino $1.76m, that was not mentioned in Fifa’s annual report, in which his salary is recorded as 4.27m Swiss francs (£3.86m).
Fifa statutes state that “the individual compensation of the Fifa president … shall be made public”. The governing body has denied wrongdoing.

“Fifa does not pay a second salary to the Fifa president and complies with all reporting requirements in relation to compensation,” it said. “The Fifa president’s annual compensation, as well as other contractual benefits, are decided by the independent compensation subcommittee.

“Fifa strongly rejects any claims that it has failed to disclose any financial information and has violated Fifa’s statutes. Fifa accounts are independently audited, and all declarations are in line with tax regulations in Switzerland, the United States and elsewhere.”

Despite these controversies, and the public opposition of the European, Asian and North and Central American and Caribbean confederations, Infantino is on course to be re-elected unopposed in March’s election.

Montagliani has rejected calls to stand against Infantino to focus on being re-elected as Concacaf’s president and Uefa has yet to find an alternative candidate despite tentatively sounding out high-profile footballing figures including Arsène Wenger and Michele Kang, who owns clubs including London City Lionesses.
The deadline for candidates to declare their intention to stand is 18 November, with the election due to be held at Fifa congress in Rabat on 18 March.

Infantino is expected to put forward a £2.6bn increase in the amount of money Fifa hands out for global football development at the meeting in Zurich, using cash from the governing body’s reserves to do so. The hike, covering funding from 2027 to 2030, would take the total Fifa spend on football development for the period to £4.83bn.

text: The three-time world champion Jillaroos maintain a strong edge but their title defence may be under threat from New Zealand and England

Four years is a long time in women’s sport. While men’s sport is ever evolving and growing, the speed of change in the women’s game is much faster, as time lost when they were sidelined in professional sport at an increasingly rapid pace is made up.

The last time the Rugby League World Cup was held, the women’s game was in a very different place. The NRLW contained just six teams, playing five rounds of competition, which was positioned almost as a sideshow to the men’s finals. Since then, it has doubled in size to 12 teams and 11 rounds, getting genuine airtime across the Australian winter.

Women’s State of Origin has also grown to a three-match series, attracting crowds of over 20,000 and broadcast reach of over two million viewers per match. While this growth certainly benefits Australia, it has also strengthened women’s rugby league across the world.

Current NRLW players feature across the majority of teams in the 2026 World Cup – not just the Jillaroos. With double the number of players in the NRLW, it has not only provided opportunities for international players to take part, but also opened pathways for Australian players from different cultural backgrounds to represent the countries their parents and grandparents hail from. While this has long been common in men’s rugby league, having more players in the NRLW provides more visibility for those players to be seen and recruited by overseas coaches for the World Cup.

Although the Jillaroos remain favourites to back up their 2022 win, in which they defeated New Zealand 54-4 in the final, the gap is closing and this is shaping up to be the closest World Cup in history. Eight teams will compete for the title – five of those return from the 2022 iteration, Australia, New Zealand, England, Papua New Guinea and France. Fiji and Wales will make their first women’s Rugby League World Cup appearances, while Samoa will compete for the first time since 2003.

Most likely to challenge the Jillaroos are New Zealand and England. The Kiwi Ferns boast a full squad of NRLW players, most notably Canberra Raiders and former Queensland Maroons halfback Zahara Temara and Sydney Roosters premiership-winning prop Otesa Pule. England have strong experience in the Super League, including nine players from the dominant Wigan Warriors. They are bolstered by the inclusion of a number of NRLW stars, with Roosters second rower Jasmin Strange certain to make a big impact.

Where the Jillaroos maintain a strong edge, though, is in the combinations they have across the team. Their squad features eight players from the Roosters – undefeated NRLW premiers in 2026 – and 13 players from the NSW Sky Blues, who won the 2026 State of Origin series in a 3-0 whitewash. Not only have these players trained and played in these combinations throughout the year, they are highly experienced at winning together. The importance of this critical mass of players coming from a strong winning culture cannot be underestimated. In high-pressure games, a team who expects to win and plays with that mindset is difficult to beat.

The Jillaroos squad also has plenty of depth, and coach Jess Skinner will have some tough decisions to make before selecting her team for the big games in this tournament. The most intriguing battle is between the two halfbacks in the squad – State of Origin-winning half Jesse Southwell and NRLW premiership-winning half Tarryn Aiken. Both are incredible talents with the ability to turn the game to their advantage. Aiken’s more recent success gives her the edge – and she has been named at halfback for the opening match against Samoa – but expect Skinner to test both players throughout the tournament.

Roosters’ and Sky Blues’ five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher has been named to make her Australian debut in the opener and is likely to hold down that spot throughout the tournament, after outstanding performances in the NRLW and State of Origin series. Her kicking game is a key strength the Jillaroos will be seeking to exploit – her pinpoint accuracy was on show in the NRLW grand final, as she troubled the opposition kick chasers and set up multiple tries for her team with her fifth tackle options. Also working in Kelleher’s favour is her combination with both Aiken at the Roosters and Southwell in the Sky Blues’ set up.

Possibly the most controversial selection call for the Jillaroos has already been made, with former captain Ali Brigginshaw missing out on selection in the squad. Brigginshaw retired from the NRLW after this year’s grand final and, after missing out on a fairytale ending with the Brisbane Broncos, would have been hoping to end her career on a high with a World Cup win. But the selectors did not have the 36-year-old in their plans and she has been left to watch the tournament unfold from the stands, while Sky Blues’ and Sydney Roosters’ captain Isabelle Kelly takes the leadership reins.

text: Black Cats can reboot season against Torreense in Europa League in a break from tough start to domestic campaign

There is a pleasing symmetry about Sunderland’s Europa League trip to Portugal to face Torreense on Thursday night. The club’s last competitive venture on European soil, 53 years ago, was the second leg of a European Cup Winners’ Cup second-round tie against Sporting in Lisbon for the FA Cup holders, then in the Second Division.

In a striking parallel, second-tier Torreense prompted widespread surprise by beating Sporting in the Portuguese Cup final last season. The reward was a place in the Europa League and their chances of reaching the next phase of the competition early next year were boosted when they beat Lillestrøm 2-1 in Norway last month.

Torreense are struggling in the league – they sit 15th with six points from seven games. They face a side who have made an underwhelming opening to the Premier League campaign featuring one win, against their fellow strugglers Fulham.

With a visit to Bournemouth, who are 18th, a place and a point below Sunderland, on Sunday, Régis Le Bris is expected to rotate his squad. Even so, it would be a minor shock if Sunderland fail to beat Torreense.

Torreense’s home ground, the Estádio Manuel Marques in Torres Vedras, 31 miles north of Lisbon, holds 2,431 spectators, falling short of Uefa regulations. This has prompted the match being switched to the medieval town of Leiria, an hour’s drive north of Torres Vedras and almost two hours from the luxury Lisbon hotel where Sunderland are basing themselves after failing to find suitable accommodation elsewhere.

Almost 4,000 Sunderland fans are travelling to the 23,888-capacity Estádio Dr Magalhães Pessoa, normally the home of second-tier União Leiria. With a limited supply of local hotel rooms, some are staying in Lisbon or Porto, while others have found lodgings in nearby towns and villages, including Fátima. A pilgrimage town, Fátima is one of the most important shrines in the Catholic world and attracts more than six million tourists every year. As visitors from Wearside sightsee in forecast bright sunshine and 25C, they may be tempted to pray for respite from a harsh north-east winter at the Stadium of Light.

Although Sunderland have played well at times this season, the failure to sign a specialist right-winger during the summer has led to Le Bris frequently fielding two natural right-backs in Trai Hume and Thomas Meunier. Hamstring injuries to Brian Brobbey and Dan Ballard have caused problems at both ends of the pitch and the previously reliable Robin Roefs has suffered a few untypical goalkeeping wobbles.

Context is required though. Sunderland’s first six league fixtures have been against the present top four – Manchester City, Arsenal, Brighton and Brentford. Nonetheless, quiet concern will segue into downright panic should the next two domestic games – at Bournemouth and then at home to Leeds – fail to produce at least one win. There is also anxiety that Malick Fofana, the £30m left-winger signed from Lyon on deadline day who is struggling to displace the erratic Nilson Angulo, may be too lightweight for England’s top tier.

On Tuesday evening, Sunderland announced their set-piece coach, James Brayne, had left and would be replaced by Thor Herdal. The 34-year-old arrives from Nordsjælland, where he was head of set pieces and analysis. He has also worked with Denmark’s national team.

Given that Sunderland travel to Poland to face Lech Poznan next Thursday, minimising travel and the attendant fatigue has become a priority. It explains why they will fly straight from Lisbon to Bournemouth on Friday.
Not that Torreense intend to merely make up the numbers. Back in the club’s home town, locals are preparing for an annual national day of celebration on 20 October.

It commemorates the role played by an imposing series of forts and military defences built in 1809-10 and known as the Lines of Torres Vedras in defending Lisbon from French invaders during the Peninsular war.
Torreense are hoping to demonstrate similarly stout resistance against a team led by a Frenchman and with several French-speaking players.

Sunderland have reason to be wary of Stopira, Torreense’s influential 38-year-old captain and left-back, who played for Cape Verde at this summer’s World Cup, and their gifted playmaker João Marques and Ghanaian striker Malik Abubakari. The challenge for Sunderland is to use this last blast of southern European warmth to revitalise a season in danger of unravelling.

text: In 1977, Richards sued to play in the US Open after transitioning. Now she supports bans on trans athletes in women’s sports. A new biography explores a complex legacy

It was a story that dominated tennis headlines back in 1977: Dr Renée Richards, an ophthalmologist who excelled as a male amateur player before a sex-change operation, was suing for the right to play in the women’s draw of the US Open. Where did Richards go for legal assistance? None other than Roy Cohn.

Better known for prosecuting suspected communists during the red scare and mentoring Donald Trump, Cohn turned his attention to fighting for Richards’s inclusion. His firm successfully argued the case – part of the narrative of a new biography, Finding Renée Richards: The Groundbreaking Story of Tennis’s Trans Pioneer by Julie Kliegman.

“The lawsuit was really significant,” Kliegman says. “Obviously, clearly, it was very significant for Renée. But the decision was limited to her, as opposed to setting a precedent for trans people going forward.”

For Kliegman – a sports journalist who is trans and non-binary – the project offered a chance to reexamine a 50-year-old cause célèbre and the topic of inclusion for trans people, in sports and in wider society, then and now.

“There are a lot of parallels,” Kliegman says. “What struck me the most is that if anything, the conversation and dynamics between athletes are amplified today by the hostility [that is] more powerful than anything Renée would have faced.”

Kliegman researched the story, in part, by accessing her subject’s multiple autobiographies as well as interview transcripts from another memoir project that never got published. They also interviewed Richards, now 92, in person multiple times. On one occasion, Richards showed Kliegman photo after photo of the celebrities who had posed with her over the years. Another time, the two met for lunch at the golf club where Richards still comes by regularly for a ladies’ day on the links.
These meetings also gave Kliegman a chance for some back-and-forth with their subject over trans rights.

“Renée today believes that trans women and girls should not be allowed to play girls and women’s sports unless they have not undergone so-called male puberty,” Kliegman says, describing this as a 180-degree shift from the lawsuit Richards filed in 1977. “She does not, overall, believe most trans athletes should be allowed to play girls and women’s sports. It was an interesting point of tension between me and Renée.”
Richards “cites research that shows trans girls and women may have an advantage over cisgender peers,” Kliegman says. “My impression is that the research isn’t conclusive enough.”
In writing the book, the author made a decision that went against their journalistic training but was in accordance with Richards’s wishes.

“In recent years, you usually don’t refer to someone by their former name, former pronouns, when they change it,” Kliegman says, “even when referring to past points of their life. I came to understand [using their birth name when talking about their early life] was really important for [Richards] to fully depict the back and forth, the push and pull, Dick [Richards was formerly called Richard Raskind] and Renée.”

The decision to use he/him pronouns in referring to Raskind, and she/her pronouns when it came to Richards, “was a tough one for me,” Kliegman says. “It goes against the journalistic norms I understand.” Yet, the author adds, “[Richards] felt I could not describe it accurately without ‘he’ and ‘her’ pronouns … So much in the book, Renée did not have any say over. It’s a journalistic project, not an authorized biography. Just about the only thing I think she needed a say over was [to] describe her respectfully.”

As the book tells it, Raskind grew up in a Jewish-American family in New York City. His father was an orthopedic surgeon, and his mother was a psychiatrist. According to the book, Raskind was bullied by his older sister, who made him wear her clothing. As he entered young adulthood, matriculating at Yale University, he voluntarily began wearing women’s clothing in private, and presenting as a female on visits to Greenwich Village. All the while, he played men’s tennis. After medical school at the University of Rochester, he became an ophthalmologist in New York, and joined the Navy, where he competed in service tennis tournaments and worked aboard submarines. Throughout college, med school and beyond, he dated women. Yet for a time, he discussed his conflict over his gender identity with several psychoanalysts.

“At the time, it was really, really difficult to get the care you needed as a trans person,” Kliegman says. “Also, on top of this, Renée was uncertain she was a woman. Certainly, she was a trans woman. Certainly, she was Renée. But there were also these other pressures encouraging her in the direction to present as Richard Raskind, whether it be for his career, for his love life, different forces.”

In the late 1960s, Raskind traveled to a clinic in Morocco that performed sex-change operations, yet decided against surgery. He subsequently met and married Barbara Mole, the woman who would become his wife and the mother of their son, Nicholas. After the marriage ended, Raskind decided to undergo a sex-change operation, this time in his home town of New York, in 1975. He chose the new first name Renée, French for “reborn”.
It was a new start in many ways: a new gender, a new name and a cross-country relocation to California. Yet Richards’s old love of tennis remained. She began competing as a woman, and having success.

“As Richard Raskind, he was a great tennis player,” Kliegman says. “He ranked as high as the top 10 in the eastern region of 35-and-over players. He was quite good, with a powerful lefty serve that people would talk about and recognize. Dick became Renée – and she remained a very good tennis player.”

Then she was outed – by broadcast journalist Richard Carlson, father of Tucker. With her background now public, Richards’s right to play women’s pro tennis was challenged by the United States Tennis Association (USTA). The organization questioned whether Richards was “genetically female”, as quoted in the book. Officials demanded a test to see whether Richards had “the conventional XX sex chromosomes”, according to the book. Eventually, Richards sued.

“Tennis is sort of the through line, one of the through lines of her life,” Kliegman says. “At any age, she could contribute to it … It sustained her through difficult times in her life. I think it’s what prompted the lawsuit – ‘Why I can’t I have this, this lifeline for me, a constant throughout my life, I should be able to play tennis, do the thing I love.’”

After a judge ruled in Richards’s favor, she was allowed to compete in the US Open. In singles, Richards lost in the first round to the defending Wimbledon champion, Virginia Wade. In doubles, Richards had more success, joining Betty Ann Stuart to reach the final, where they lost to Martina Navratilova and Betty Stöve.
The difficulties for Richards did not end. Some female competitors treated her with hostility. The book credits Billie Jean King with convincing most of the women’s tennis world to let Richards play.

“Billie Jean King was a huge part of Renée’s story,” Kliegman says. “She took a little while to make up her mind. She was quiet on the issue for so many years, but I understand why … She ended up calling doctors, asking them questions. She was not super familiar with the concept of trans people at the time.

“She also met with Renée, which I think was really crucial … It convinced [King] that [Richards] was a woman like any other, who deserved a place on the tour. Billie Jean King showed support by playing doubles alongside Renée … which was huge, I think.”

After retiring from professional tennis, she was ranked at No 20 in singles at her peak, Richards went on to coach Navratilova in what the book describes as a successful but sometimes bumpy partnership. Richards also returned to practicing ophthalmology for a long career, with a list of clients that included sports and politics journalist Keith Olbermann. There was a late-in-life tragedy for Richards: her son Nicholas died by suicide at age 47 in 2019.
“It’s still raw for her,” Kliegman says. “I don’t think the tragedy of losing a child is something most people ever get over.”

As Kliegman has gotten to know Richards, the author reflects that there is a little less daylight between their positions on trans rights, in part because of anti-trans policies of the Trump administration.

“If I did not see her views on trans athletes themselves evolve, what I did see was that she now understands restrictions on trans athletes … are connected to this broader project the right wing has to try to eliminate trans people from public life,” Kliegman says. “It’s not a distinction she was making, and was comfortable with, before Trump was reelected.”

text: Tucked away on a Peak District hillside is The Maynard, bursting with memorabilia and stories left by touring teams

As the modern cricketer hops from Crowne Plaza to Holiday Inn, well rewarded and with plenty of time for golf, he or she might feel perfectly content. But life has not always been a merry-go-round of air-con and airports.

Hop off the train at Grindleford, where homemade bunting loops along the platform fence, highlighting books about trains in this national year of reading, and you are in the Peak District. There has been early morning rain and the trees, damply beautiful, are on the turn. Golden beech, rusty horse chestnut, hues of greens and yellows, disappear up the slopes of Padley Gorge and into the valleys.

Five minutes along Station Road, past the Station Cafe, a favourite for hikers and famous for its huge mugs of tea, and you arrive at The Maynard, once the Maynard Arms, host to international touring cricket teams in the middle of the last century when they played Derbyshire and Yorkshire. In the snug, tucked in behind the reception desk and the bar, is a small homage to teams past, autographs, bats, black and white photos of young men, nearly all now gone.

According to the caption accompanying the team photo, Australia first stayed here in 1930 to escape the noise of Sheffield, then a city of steelworks and smoking chimneys. A young Don Bradman, just 21, stares back in his blazer from the front row, legs stretched out, arms crossed. He is part way through a magical summer that included 334 against England at Headingley, 1,000 runs by the end of May and 974 runs in the Ashes series.

Australia returned to Grindleford in 1938, unpacking their suitcases for 10 days, from 28 June to 7 July, playing against Derbyshire at Queen’s Park, Chesterfield, and Yorkshire at Bramall Lane, Sheffield, when only rain prevented the hosts pulling off a famous victory.

“Tremendous furnaces paint the night sky with rosy brilliance for many square miles on the northern and eastern sides of Sheffield,” writes “Easel” in the Maitland Mercury on 21 July that year, “but when the train emerges at Grindleford from the long tunnel, it enters a haven of rest where nothing but beauty meets the eye and greets the senses, ideal conditions for the Australian team to return to after their strenuous days of cricket.”

The Australians were much admired on that tour, but they were not perfect house guests. The rumours about Lindsay Hassett smuggling a complaining goat from the nearby hills into his room, to the dismay of his roommates, Stan McCabe and Bill O’Reilly, appear to be true.

There is corroborating evidence from the Albany Advertiser, which wrote: “The goat, with a goat’s extraordinary taste in food, reduced McCabe’s bedroom to a remarkable condition, much to the delight of that rascal Hassett.” Jack Fingleton remembered the incident in his book Cricket Crisis: “The next night everybody locked their doors, which was just as well because Hassett found a hedgehog.”

The escapade was not enough to put the hotel off naming 15 rooms after the players. You can stay in the (Chuck) Fleetwood-Smith or the (Ben) Barnett, the Fingleton or the (Jack) Badcock. The gorgeous bridal suite, complete with roll top bath and enormous wooden bed looking out of a huge window over the hills, is named after Bradman – and his nearly perfect average. There are also rooms named after Hugh Tayfield, Percy Mansell, George Fullerton and Syd Pegler, members and manager of the South Africa side of 1951.

After the war years, the next Australia team to land on these shores was Bradman’s Invincibles of 1948, who completed their tour of England without losing a game, drawing with Yorkshire and defeating Derbyshire by an innings. They, too, stayed at The Maynard and were said to have bathed in the nearby river Derwent.

The Rev Keith Bamford, speaking to the Derbyshire Cricket Foundation as part of a heritage project, told them: “Keith Miller was there in 1948 and apparently spent a little too long in the bar one night and missed the bus to Sheffield. A journalist there lent him £10 for a taxi, didn’t see any repayment for years and years, and many years later in Melbourne he was sitting watching the Test. Miller tapped him on the shoulder and gave him some money and said ‘that’s for Grindleford.’”

The dates are slightly different, but it is a memory backed up by the journalist, Basil Easterbrook, writing in the Sunday Sun of 17 June, 1973. “Once in 1953, I was staying with the Australian Team at the Maynard Arms. Lindsay Hassett, the captain and George Davies, the manager, went off to London for a few days break and Keith Miller was left in charge. Nugget shared a room with Lindwall and on the second morning due to an oversight they received no early call.

“At 11am, Australia’s two great opening bowlers were peeling off their pyjamas at the Maynard Arms, while several miles away they were just closing the gates on 30,000 Yorkshiremen waiting for battle to recommence at 11.30.

“Hire a car Bas,” shouted Miller, as he and Lindwall fell about the bedroom trying to climb into their trousers. I got a Rolls-Royce from the local undertaker – the only vehicle available – and the three of us drove in some state up to the edge of the moors and then down the rim of the saucer that is Sheffield. We pulled up outside Bramall Lane at 11.28.”

In this version, Easterbrook gets his money back 19 years later, via Ray Lindwall, “older, heavier, greying of hair, but the smile and the eyes the same”, pushing a fiver into the breast pocket of his jacket.

Local historian Alan Jacques, who was born above the village shop in Grindleford in 1951, remembers going to The Maynard for autographs from the 1965 South Africans, the last side to tour before isolation. “Some of them came out and asked us where was a good place to walk and we took them down to the riverside.”

He still has his autograph book from 1963, too, which contains scribbles from four of the visiting West Indians – Lance Gibbs, Alf Valentine, Seymour Nurse and Deryck Murray – who were sitting on the wall outside the hotel

These days, though the local cricket club comes in for drinks and events, touring teams choose hotels with sharper corners and city footprints. Perhaps they could again be tempted to build in a few days break at the Noosa of hiking boots and peachy dawns. As Ian Johnson wrote for the Adelaide’s The News in 1953: “It’s a very comfortable country pub on the side of a very lovely valley which allows the players a perfect rest.”
This is an extract from the Guardian’s weekly cricket email, The Spin. To subscribe, just visit this page and follow the instructions.

news.title: Athletics wishes it could scrub the women’s marathon world record – what can be done? | Sean Ingle
news.desc: Ruth Chepngetich’s failed doping test, five months after she obliterated the record in 2024, left the sport deeply uneasy but powerless to act When Ruth Chepngetich annihilated the women’s marathon world record in Chicago two years ago today, NBC’s commentators compared it to the moon landing . “Bring it on Neil Armstrong!” cried one. “She has done things in this sport that we have not seen,” said another. “Unbelievable!” That was a word others reached for too after the Kenyan had crossed the line in 2hr 9min 56sec, a time that not only smashed the world record by 1min 57sec, but her personal
text: Ruth Chepngetich’s failed doping test, five months after she obliterated the record in 2024, left the sport deeply uneasy but powerless to act

When Ruth Chepngetich annihilated the women’s marathon world record in Chicago two years ago today, NBC’s commentators compared it to the moon landing. “Bring it on Neil Armstrong!” cried one. “She has done things in this sport that we have not seen,” said another. “Unbelievable!”

That was a word others reached for too after the Kenyan had crossed the line in 2hr 9min 56sec, a time that not only smashed the world record by 1min 57sec, but her personal best by a staggering five minutes. Afterwards she was asked by Robert Johnson of Let’s Run what her response was to those who believed she must be doping. “People must talk,” she replied. “I don’t know.”

We know a lot more now. Because five months after that epic run, Chepngetich’s star came crashing down to earth. First she failed a doping test. Then she was banned for three years. These days people in the sport talk about her reluctantly, like a family member who has joined a mysterious cult. Yet her world record still stands because she passed a test after the race itself.
What should we think of this? What are we allowed legally to say about this? And what, if anything, can be done about it?

A couple of weeks ago, I spoke to Brett Clothier, the head of the Athletics Integrity Unit, which prosecuted the case against Chepngetich, to ask about her world record. “It is not satisfactory, to be frank,” he admitted. “But the world anti-doping code is pretty clearcut on the rights athletes have, even if they’re found guilty of a doping offence.”
That much is true. But while legally Chepngetich was clean when she broke her world record, the fact it stands surely damages the sport’s credibility.

True, there are plenty of highly suspicious records from the 80s and early 90s, given what we know about state-sponsored doping behind the iron curtain and in China. And if you believe Florence Griffith Joyner knocked more than half a second off her 100m and 200m times in 1988 by doing 5,000 sit-ups a day and drinking water, I have some magic beans to sell you.

Griffith Joyner, of course, never tested positive. But before her death aged 38, her fellow American sprinter Darrell Robinson claimed in a paid interview with the German magazine Stern that he had sold her human growth hormone for $2,000.

He also alleged that she had told him: “If you want to make a million dollars, you’ve got to invest a couple of thousand.” Yet as much as Flo-Jo’s records make us uneasy, they are seen as coming from a bygone and more lawless era.
Also, what makes Chepngetich unique is that no other athlete has been hit with a lengthy ban so soon after a world record.

The Kenyan’s defence for being 20 times the legal limit of hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) in her system? That she had taken her housemaid’s medication after feeling hot and having a rapid resting heartbeat. It was, the AIU noted, a “hardly credible” explanation.

The AIU also found screenshots on Chepngetich’s phone about the banned drug testosterone and “messages related to unidentified third parties working on ‘programs’ possibly related to doping”. The Kenyan has insisted that she has never used testosterone and the messages were from a group chat, but they hardly inspire confidence either.

So what can be done? The short answer, having spoken to the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), is very little. As a Wada spokesperson pointed out to me, removing her results before her positive test “in the absence of any evidence or reasonable inference that the athlete was doping before or at the time of the earlier results, might well breach a number of legal principles including proportionality and human rights.”

But what about Lance Armstrong, who was stripped of his Tour de France titles despite not being convicted of breaking any doping rules while competing? Could this not apply here? Not according to Wada.

“He had procedural avenues open to him to contest the sanction but ultimately chose not to use them,” a spokesperson told me. “That makes his case a relatively weak precedent for establishing how far retrospective disqualification could legally go.”

One idea I floated to various experts was the idea that athletes could be asked to sign a social contract, which pledged they would accept losing their world record if they tested positive within a year of that world record or winning an Olympic medal.

In theory, one anti-doping expert put it to me, it was possible to do this. But he felt it would require everybody – from sports federations and governments to athlete bodies and human rights groups – to buy in and to agree to change the Wada code to allow retrospective punishments. And that is not going to happen.

At least track and field can point to many significant victories over doping in the last decade, given that Chepngetich is one of 317 elite Kenyan athletes the AIU has caught since it was set up in 2017. Many sports pay lip service to catching cheats. Athletics actually does. And the AIU does it on a modest budget of $11.9m (£9m) a year.

There are also positive signs that prominent athletes realise more must be done when it comes to anti-doping. Before Sabastian Sawe set his men’s marathon world record in London, for instance, his sponsors, Adidas, paid $50,000 for extra testing. Nike did the same for two of their athletes, Jacob Kiplimo and Brigid Kosgei, before Chicago.

Sawe’s agent, Eric Lilot, wants to go further by making his athletes sign a contract that will require them to give up any money still owed to them if it is shown they intentionally tried to dope. All that points to brighter days ahead, however much Chepngetich’s record makes us feel queasy.

text: The three-time world champion Jillaroos maintain a strong edge but their title defence may be under threat from New Zealand and England

Four years is a long time in women’s sport. While men’s sport is ever evolving and growing, the speed of change in the women’s game is much faster, as time lost when they were sidelined in professional sport at an increasingly rapid pace is made up.

The last time the Rugby League World Cup was held, the women’s game was in a very different place. The NRLW contained just six teams, playing five rounds of competition, which was positioned almost as a sideshow to the men’s finals. Since then, it has doubled in size to 12 teams and 11 rounds, getting genuine airtime across the Australian winter.

Women’s State of Origin has also grown to a three-match series, attracting crowds of over 20,000 and broadcast reach of over two million viewers per match. While this growth certainly benefits Australia, it has also strengthened women’s rugby league across the world.

Current NRLW players feature across the majority of teams in the 2026 World Cup – not just the Jillaroos. With double the number of players in the NRLW, it has not only provided opportunities for international players to take part, but also opened pathways for Australian players from different cultural backgrounds to represent the countries their parents and grandparents hail from. While this has long been common in men’s rugby league, having more players in the NRLW provides more visibility for those players to be seen and recruited by overseas coaches for the World Cup.

Although the Jillaroos remain favourites to back up their 2022 win, in which they defeated New Zealand 54-4 in the final, the gap is closing and this is shaping up to be the closest World Cup in history. Eight teams will compete for the title – five of those return from the 2022 iteration, Australia, New Zealand, England, Papua New Guinea and France. Fiji and Wales will make their first women’s Rugby League World Cup appearances, while Samoa will compete for the first time since 2003.

Most likely to challenge the Jillaroos are New Zealand and England. The Kiwi Ferns boast a full squad of NRLW players, most notably Canberra Raiders and former Queensland Maroons halfback Zahara Temara and Sydney Roosters premiership-winning prop Otesa Pule. England have strong experience in the Super League, including nine players from the dominant Wigan Warriors. They are bolstered by the inclusion of a number of NRLW stars, with Roosters second rower Jasmin Strange certain to make a big impact.

Where the Jillaroos maintain a strong edge, though, is in the combinations they have across the team. Their squad features eight players from the Roosters – undefeated NRLW premiers in 2026 – and 13 players from the NSW Sky Blues, who won the 2026 State of Origin series in a 3-0 whitewash. Not only have these players trained and played in these combinations throughout the year, they are highly experienced at winning together. The importance of this critical mass of players coming from a strong winning culture cannot be underestimated. In high-pressure games, a team who expects to win and plays with that mindset is difficult to beat.

The Jillaroos squad also has plenty of depth, and coach Jess Skinner will have some tough decisions to make before selecting her team for the big games in this tournament. The most intriguing battle is between the two halfbacks in the squad – State of Origin-winning half Jesse Southwell and NRLW premiership-winning half Tarryn Aiken. Both are incredible talents with the ability to turn the game to their advantage. Aiken’s more recent success gives her the edge – and she has been named at halfback for the opening match against Samoa – but expect Skinner to test both players throughout the tournament.

Roosters’ and Sky Blues’ five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher has been named to make her Australian debut in the opener and is likely to hold down that spot throughout the tournament, after outstanding performances in the NRLW and State of Origin series. Her kicking game is a key strength the Jillaroos will be seeking to exploit – her pinpoint accuracy was on show in the NRLW grand final, as she troubled the opposition kick chasers and set up multiple tries for her team with her fifth tackle options. Also working in Kelleher’s favour is her combination with both Aiken at the Roosters and Southwell in the Sky Blues’ set up.

Possibly the most controversial selection call for the Jillaroos has already been made, with former captain Ali Brigginshaw missing out on selection in the squad. Brigginshaw retired from the NRLW after this year’s grand final and, after missing out on a fairytale ending with the Brisbane Broncos, would have been hoping to end her career on a high with a World Cup win. But the selectors did not have the 36-year-old in their plans and she has been left to watch the tournament unfold from the stands, while Sky Blues’ and Sydney Roosters’ captain Isabelle Kelly takes the leadership reins.

text: The Test series shapes as one of unforced errors and modest scores with both sides unconvincing with the bat and relying on their bowling attack

Lost among the looking back to Australia’s Test tour of South Africa in 2018, there lies a similarity to the team about to take on that challenge in 2026. The previous side relied on a primo bowling quartet of Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Mitchell Starc, along with David Warner’s power as opener and the middle-order ballast of Steve Smith. The rest of the batting was makeshift: Cameron Bancroft the recently added opener, Usman Khawaja with at that stage a parlous record away from home, and the Marsh brothers an entirely unknowable quantity at five and six.

This time around, the same four bowlers have burnished their careers by a further 998 Test wickets, the proven batting still consists of one aggressive left-handed opener plus Smith, and Australia otherwise remain makeshift.

Matt Renshaw has done good things against the white ball, but his preparation to be the country’s new opener in Durban has consisted of one innings against Bangladesh in Mackay. Marnus Labuschagne reassured with a warm-up century, but that game was so relaxed that he might have played in flip-flops. Cameron Green was an issue until two Test innings ago, then having finally produced a performance of note, got injured. That means Beau Webster will be bowling cover, with one of Cooper Connolly or Nic Maddinson to get Green’s job with the bat.

A choice between those two options is truly bizarre. Granted, Connolly is a talent with a knack for nailing an entrance: his fourth Big Bash game, his fourth List A match, and his first-class debut all came in tournament finals, and each time he made a contribution to yet another trophy heading west.

Still, Connolly has played little first-class cricket since, never exceeding his 90 on debut, while his long-format bowling has been a non-event. He had no claim to making a Test squad in Sri Lanka in 2025, a pick that led to one of the cheapest baggy greens ever handed out, for a match in which he was so peripheral that he might as well have been the boundary sponge. In 2026 to date he has played one first-class match, made 10 and 10, and yet another squad spot given on potential rather than performance has seen another Test chance open up for him. The 23-year-old could well be the future, but has never yet demonstrated that he is the present.

Maddinson, meanwhile, is the past. It is bewildering how many cricket people in the last few days have cited him being highly regarded in his youth, as though that affects a 34-year-old today. He deserves all the goodwill in the world for overcoming cancer and getting back to the game, but goodwill doesn’t come bundled with a Test cap. If you think Connolly is light on for first-class cricket, Maddinson hasn’t played since March 2025, when he made 4 and 0 at the end of a season averaging 17. According to selectors, it was the season before that, the one that started three years ago, that had the good juice.

“From 2018 to 2024, he was one of the leading players in Shield cricket,” was national coach Andrew McDonald’s defence of their call. Of which, with the full measure of respect than it deserves, so what? Bill Ponsford led the runs from 1924 to 1928, and he’s not getting a centennial call-up. Players have to play the game to prove that they can play the game, especially with the intense demands of delivering high-level skill over the course of five days. Nobody knows if Maddinson can even field for that long, let alone be effective with the bat.

You could claim Smith as precedent, given he slotted back in after 16 months following his “sandpaper ban”. But Smith already had the record of a batting great. It is something else to point to runs that weren’t enough to get a player into the Australian side when he was making them, but subsequently demand his selection years after the fact, accruing interest like bearer bonds.

None of this is Maddinson’s fault, nor Connolly’s. Their inclusions reflect a chicken-and-egg batting scenario of difficult conditions and mediocre returns, whereby Australian state cricket has no clear next contenders demanding a spot. In that economy, vibes outweigh output, so players can get picked on being a highly rated young talent – never mind whether that rating was first noted in 2023 or 2013.

The good news for Australia is that South Africa have a similar side: unconvincing batting, relying on the bowling attack to shore it up. Their 18-man squad was due to have been trimmed by now, but they are giving pace leader Kagiso Rabada every minute to overcome his hamstring injury. If he doesn’t, there are options: Corbin Bosch to join Marco Jansen and Anrich Nortje in a pace trio; Simon Harmer instead of Bosch in a spin duo with Keshav Maharaj; or all of the above if Jansen’s batting form sees South Africa put him at No 7. Wiaan Mulder offers all-round seam, and might be a better batting option than the out-of-sorts Tristan Stubbs in any case.

This shapes as a series of unforced errors and modest scores, with the spoils going to whoever can cobble together enough of a redoubt while building on sand. It will be an exercise in nerve-holding and a bit of hand-holding. The outcome matters, beyond even pride, in moving either side far closer to another spot in a World Test Championship final, the decider where they faced off last year. South Africa always feel the pressure to prove themselves, Australia would like to move the past further hence, and Smith could slay a demon or two. However it goes, it will at least let the 2026 teams tell us a story more recent than the heavy-trodden mud of eight years since.

op.title: What’s left to say about Australia’s ball-tampering? The answer is everything | Geoff Lemon
