text: The story from the 2018 Test in South Africa will stay alive for years more, unless it is finally put to sleep with the truth of what happened

Add it to the immeasurable list of things that you can blame Covid for. Without the pandemic, Australia’s Test team would have headed to South Africa in February 2021, less than three years after the 2018 sandpaper scandal saw them come home from Johannesburg in disarray. With memories fresh, the attention would have been intense on the returning players: headlined by sacked captain Steve Smith, his replacement Tim Paine, and principal antagonist David Warner, with a support act of bowlers Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Mitchell Starc.

At least, though, that prompt rematch would have lanced the boil of Australian cricket’s great modern humiliation, after Cameron Bancroft was caught sandpapering the match ball in the third Test at Cape Town. Instead, a lack of appetite for pandemic-era touring saw Cricket Australia cancel the 2021 tour before kicking a replacement years down the road, and while there have been white-ball trips in the interim, it has now taken eight years for an Australian Test return to supersede their ill-starred previous visit.

Eight years. Two Olympiads. Two Fifa World Cups. About 15 World Cups of various types in cricket. All this time later, the sandpaper story still dominates the lead-up to this series. Contributing to its presence is that, against the odds of sporting mortality, while Warner and Paine are long gone, Smith and all four bowlers remain.

The slew of retrospectives has understandably given rise to sandpaper fatigue, audiences tired of hearing about an old story before a new series, while others do historical revisions. Various pundits have suggested that the bans for the players involved were an overreaction, a position that has merit given the prevalence of ball-tampering in the sport, but ignores the press conference in which Smith and Bancroft foolishly lied to cover theirs up. Other observers have argued that whatever the details, the story is so old as to be dead. “What’s left to come out after eight years?” asked Starc this week.

The answer is everything, because nothing ever really has. Every player and staff member from 2018 publicly maintains the uncomfortable truce that was struck a few days in: that no Australian players had ball-tampered before that match, and that nobody knew beyond the three charged. A farcically shallow investigation allowed Cricket Australia (CA) to arrive at these most convenient conclusions and thus avoid looking further for anything less palatable.

This is why an old story remains live, twitching like a severed electrical cable. CA’s disciplinary report identified Warner as the instigator, Bancroft as the patsy, and Smith as the leader who failed to curtail them, but no player has ever acknowledged in plain language what actually happened, either on tour or that day. The closest was the 2021 statement from the four bowlers insisting that they didn’t know about the plan, but even then, they haven’t said who did. They haven’t said who didn’t. No player has said that any of the coaches knew, or didn’t know. Everyone has been politely vague to avoid the impression of finger-pointing, and hoped the story will go away.

Warner, meanwhile, has implied for years that he was hard done by. In the past week he has been busily back at it, with a range of social media posts and replies again trying to inject ambiguity into the idea that he was principally responsible. And yet, he continues to withhold any information that would back up that claim. His former teammates won’t name Warner, and Warner won’t name them. Stories only go away when we solve the mysteries of their plots, and the wait for this one goes on.

As for what we know now, despite its ad nauseam nature, the sandpaper debacle may overall be something to be thankful for. Not in the case of Bancroft, the one player who truly lost, with an Australian career that never recovered and a domestic one that sputters like sleep apnoea. But it may have been good for the Australian team, knocking on the head the obsession with tough-bastard bluster that made previous champion sides so unlikeable.

Instead, there is now a tranche of players who, to foreign audiences steeped in the past, come across as disconcertingly affable. They may still attract angst for their performance, but less so for personality. England supporters did try raging at Cummins and Alex Carey after the Lord’s Test in 2023, but hating two of the most quietly decent characters in the game is a tough sell. On the field, decency has cost nothing in the way of results: keeping the Ashes in England twice, winning them in Australia twice, developing a compelling rivalry when India visit, Test series wins in four other countries, and pocketing two flavours of World Cup plus a Test Championship along the way.

The change in cultural style would not have been possible without the culture shock that preceded it, and the rare shared acknowledgment that the national team’s slate needed a damp cloth. With luck, after the callbacks demanded by the upcoming series, the sandpaper story can continue to recede, and the cultural gains that followed it can continue to be banked. Still, the players involved should know that truths don’t rest until their names are spoken. This story will stay alive for years more, unless it is finally put to sleep.

op.title: Sandpaper made Australia the story in 2018 while South Africa’s achievement faded into irrelevance
op.desc: The hosts’ stunning Test victory was overshadowed by the scale of national angst felt in Australia after the team’s ball tampering For South African cricketers, administrators and supporters, the most surprising aspect of the Sandpaper scandal was not that it happened. After all, the ball had been suspiciously reverse-swinging during the first two Tests of that ill-fated series in 2018. The atmosphere had turned febrile after a stairwell bust-up between Quinton de Kock and David Warner in Durban and after supporters directed misogynistic abuse at Warner and his family in Gqeberha. Nathan Lyon
text: The hosts’ stunning Test victory was overshadowed by the scale of national angst felt in Australia after the team’s ball tampering

For South African cricketers, administrators and supporters, the most surprising aspect of the Sandpaper scandal was not that it happened. After all, the ball had been suspiciously reverse-swinging during the first two Tests of that ill-fated series in 2018. The atmosphere had turned febrile after a stairwell bust-up between Quinton de Kock and David Warner in Durban and after supporters directed misogynistic abuse at Warner and his family in Gqeberha. Nathan Lyon had promised before the tour to “head-butt the line” of what was acceptable. Darren Lehmann, then Australia’s coach, came from an old school where bullying was sugar-coated with the phrase “mental disintegration”.
No, what surprised South Africans most was the scale of the fallout, and how one tiny piece of sandpaper could cause so much national angst.

Australia’s prime minister weighed in. Steve Smith and Warner were stripped of the captaincy and vice-captaincy and banned for a year. Cameron Bancroft, the 25-year-old who many believed was press-ganged into the act, received nine months. Lehmann resigned. Smith was marched through Johannesburg airport surrounded by police and cameras before breaking down in tears at a press conference in Sydney, his father standing behind him.
To Australians, this was a national disgrace. A sign of how far the team, perhaps even the country, had fallen. To many South Africans, the response was surreal.
“We thought it would be a big news story and then blow over,” says Faf du Plessis, who was South Africa’s captain in 2018.

Du Plessis is uniquely qualified to weigh in. Between making his Test debut in 2012 and the series in 2018, Du Plessis was twice found guilty of ball tampering. First, against Pakistan in 2013, he was caught rubbing the ball on his zipper. Then, in 2016 in Australia, he was seen applying saliva to the ball while sucking a mint in a brief but inflammatory furore known as “mintgate”.
His response to the 2018 scandal was therefore not outrage but recognition. “It’s a pressure cooker, isn’t it?” Du Plessis says. “You’re under so much pressure that eventually the lid blows off.”

There is an obvious temptation to draw a moral distinction between Australian and South African cricket, to present the tourists as villains and the hosts as innocents. That would be too neat and also inaccurate.

The treatment of Warner’s wife, Candice, was disgraceful. Two Cricket South Africa (CSA) officials were photographed smiling alongside supporters wearing Sonny Bill Williams masks designed to humiliate her. Kagiso Rabada, South Africa’s leading wicket-taker across the series, was initially suspended after making contact with Smith while celebrating his dismissal. CSA responded by roping in one of the country’s leading advocates, who successfully argued on appeal for the charge to be downgraded. South Africa were not above the muck. They were knee-deep in it.

But perhaps that is precisely why the Australian reaction seemed so extraordinary from across the Indian Ocean. South Africa’s Vernon Philander, who played all four Tests, still believes the punishment handed to Smith and Warner was “a little bit outrageous”. He was even more perplexed by the political intervention. “For a prime minister to get involved … I don’t think there was a need for that,” he says.

South Africans may have been less inclined to regard ball tampering as an existential offence. Michael Atherton, Sachin Tendulkar and Shahid Afridi are among the cricketers who have been handed sanctions over the condition of the ball. None prompted anything resembling the crisis that engulfed Australia in 2018.

This is not to minimise what Australia did. Sandpaper was a particularly brazen means of altering the ball and the attempts to conceal what happened compounded the offence. Yet the scale of the humiliation troubled Du Plessis. He had particular sympathy for Bancroft in only his eighth Test. “That’s not on him,” Du Plessis says. “He’s not the guy that instigated this.”
There was another reason South Africans experienced the whole episode differently. While Australia were undergoing a national crisis, the hosts were achieving something they had waited 48 years for.

They had beaten Australia away three times in succession but, since readmission, never at home. For Du Plessis’s generation, Australia were the benchmark and the antagonist – the opponent he describes as South Africa’s “Ashes”. And this was no ordinary victory. Rabada took 23 wickets. Aiden Markram scored two centuries. AB de Villiers produced a masterpiece in Gqeberha. Du Plessis made a hundred in Johannesburg with a broken finger before Philander took six wickets as Australia were crushed by 492 runs. South Africa won the series 3-1.
It should have been remembered as one of the crowning achievements in South African cricket. Instead, eight years later, the series has a one-word shorthand: “Sandpapergate.”

Australia return to South Africa this week for their first Test series in the country since. Pat Cummins now leads a team that presents a markedly different face to the one that arrived in 2018. South Africa have changed too. Having triumphed in the World Test Championship final last year, they are no longer burdened by the same insecurities against Australia.

But the demons and difficult conversations from 2018 still loom large. Australia looked at that act of sporting dishonesty and saw something much larger reflected back. South Africa looked at the same piece of sandpaper and watched one of their greatest victories disappear behind it.

text: The Roosters winger completed a clean sweep of honours in two years as he heads back to union with Japanese club Saitama
“Mark’s a bit of an adventurer,” the Roosters coach, Trent Robinson, volunteered about his departing winger Mark Nawaqanitawase, perhaps the most-liked player in the NRL, after his final appearance.

The 26-year-old has completed rugby league in a little more than two years, having secured a premiership in Sunday’s grand final, to go along with State of Origin and Kangaroos accolades. He finished with an extraordinary 47 tries in 47 NRL matches, including seven in his last four.

An adventurer. It’s a description that should not come as a surprise given Nawaqanitawase’s unorthodox approach to the wing position. Though, yes, the coach was referring to the decision by the code-hopper to sign a two-year contract with Japanese rugby union club Saitama.

“He’s always going to travel and play in those different codes,” Robinson continued. “But I wouldn’t be surprised if you see him back one day. I feel like he’s made a big difference to us. And we’ve also made a big difference to him.”

It has been barely two years since the former – and likely future – Wallaby showed up at Moore Park. Back then, his “arms were painted on” and he “could not tackle”, Robinson joked. The coach was comfortable ribbing his player in public largely because Nawaqanitawase’s brilliance is now without question.

The grand final was more proof. Two tries. Almost two more. At least half a dozen moments that would be the highlight of many other wingers’ seasons. While other Roosters were booed by the stadium filled largely with Newcastle supporters, the cheers for Nawaqanitawase emphasised the impact this extraordinary athlete has made in his two full seasons in the NRL.

“When he gets the ball, you sort of go: ‘OK, um, what’s going to happen here? What can he do?’,” Robinson said. “When other people get the ball in the same situation, you sort of know what’s going to happen. When Mark gets it, there’s like this energy that ‘OK, he can do something here’, always. And he believes he can do something always.”

In the first half he leaped so high for a ball, when he came down his knee hit the face of Greg Marzhew, rotating Nawaqanitawase towards the touchline. The angle of his re-entry was exacerbated by the impact of Kalyn Ponga, forcing the winger’s reaching arm to drop the ball for his first near-miss.

Not long after, Nawaqanitawase’s aerial dominance was obvious again, when the winger easily batted back another kick towards his teammates. What followed was the highlight of the match, and the Roosters winger was central, even though it was Ponga who had picked up Nawaqanitawase’s deflection to run the length of the field for a Newcastle try.

These were warning signs for Nawaqanitawase’s ensuing explosion. A ball from Rob Toia bounced towards him, and he kicked it forward three times, the kind of touch that would be ridiculed in the round ball game unless it led to a goal. Sure enough, the winger regathered for the crucial first Roosters try after a bewildering first half they had dominated without – until then – reward. It was a frankly ridiculous four-pointer, that looked borderline accidental. But that’s Nawaqanitawase, on a crusade to upend expectation.

His presence in a Roosters team not widely liked helped ease the sadness as the Tricolours edged out the underdog Knights. Newcastle’s forwards were slowly undone by the assault, and their famous strike-from-anywhere attack led by Ponga had been quelled by the sliding Roosters centres Billy Smith and Toia, keeping the Knights to just two linebreaks.

Another Nawaqanitawase try followed in the second half, and the winger came close on two more occasions. Even when he was not within reach of the line, the late offloads and audacious kicks, a tiptoe down the sideline, even the tough carries for which he has increasingly become known, were each a decoration to his own farewell party.

The NRL world is partly in mourning about his departure, while the remainder are in disbelief union might have got one over them. His contract with Saitama, with a reported annual salary of $1.4m, was eye-watering when it was first revealed in January. After his exploits in recent months, it’s starting to look like a steal.

Of course, Robinson wants Nawaqanitawase to return to the Roosters after his two years in Japan, which neatly bookend next year’s home Rugby World Cup. Even if he does not come back to the NRL, however, the past two years will not soon be forgotten. They are a testament to the freakish brilliance of a player of his own protoype.

“I’m just trying to think of a winger that’s had as bigger impact,” Robinson said. “What Mark’s done from the wing, wingers touching the ball in so many different types and styles and that. I hope he’s created another generation of those types of players.”

news.title: Real Madrid's Vinicius Jr banned for four games and will miss El Clasico vs. Barcelona
news.desc: The Brazilian winger was sent off during the last home game against Villarreal after pulling Nathan Saliba's hair before scoring
text: Real Madrid forward Vinicius Jr. will miss El Clasico against FC Barcelona on Oct. 25 after being suspended for four games for the red card he received in Real Madrid's last home game, against Villarreal at the Bernabeu. The Brazilian forward came on in the 52nd minute and was sent off 20 minutes later. Vinicius Jr. thought he had scored, and Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho celebrated alongside his team and ran over to him a few seconds before VAR ruled out the goal and sent him off. The VAR check showed Vinicius Jr. had pulled Nathan Saliba's hair before scoring. The Spanish Football Federation's rules state that pulling an opponent's hair is violent conduct, and Vinicius was suspended for the upcoming four Real Madrid matches against Sevilla, Barcelona, Racing Santander and Valencia. The federation's competition committee gave Vinicius a two-game ban for "violent conduct, without the possibility of playing the ball" and two additional games "for arguing with the referee with an aggressive attitude and having to be restrained by his teammates." Mourinho, who skipped Saturday's post-match press conference after the episode, spoke ahead of the Champions League match against AS Roma on Wednesday and said, "After the previous match against Atletico Madrid in which Vinicius started, I decided to take a different approach and to protect him a little and then bring him on when the game called for a player like Vini. I think that worked out well: the stadium, which had sometimes voiced disapproval, immediately rallied behind him the moment he started warming up. I believe that was a crucial turning point for him. He came on and played very well, the goal and the sending off were a shame, of course, but it seemed like something clicked for him, reigniting that joy and reminding him of the kind of player he truly is." The ban applies only to domestic competitions, so Vinicius will be able to play against AS Roma on Wednesday, then against RB Leipzig and on Nov. 4 against AEK Athens. He will be eligible to play in LaLiga again only after the November international break, when Real Madrid meet Celta Vigo on Nov. 22.
