news.title: U.S. Soccer to launch Arthur M. Blank Crest Cup for women's clubs; initial prize pool set at $1.5 million
news.desc: There is currently no launch date for the Crest Cup but U.S. Soccer hopes to have the competition up and running before the 2031 Women's World Cup, which is expected to take place in North America
text: U.S. Soccer will launch the Arthur M. Blank Crest Cup, a first-of-its-kind women's competition in the country that will see clubs across different leagues compete with each other for a prize pool of $1.5 million. There is currently no start date for the Crest Cup, but U.S. Soccer intends to have the competition up and running by the 2031 Women's World Cup, which will likely be hosted jointly by the U.S., Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica. Teams from the NWSL and the Gainbridge Super League will take part in the inaugural edition of the event, though other clubs could join the fold at some point. "It'll for sure be the NWSL teams and the GSL teams and we're looking at the option for lower division professional teams being able to join, as well as amateur women's teams being able to join and what that could and should look like but we're also not of the thought that the tournament can't evolve," U.S. Soccer president Cindy Parlow Cone told select members of the media this week. "Maybe we start with the NWSL and GSL, and then evolve and engage the other teams, right?" The tournament will resemble the Lamar Hunt U.S. Open Cup, the century-old men's club competition, and other similar cup competitions around the world such as the FA Cup. Parlow Cone admitted she had a longtime interest in launching a women's equivalent in the U.S. and has finally been able to follow through with the idea because of the increasingly robust nature of women's club soccer at the professional and amateur levels nationwide. "I have wanted to launch this competition for quite some time," Parlow Cone said. "Historically, we haven't had a robust women's amateur league and competition and a number of teams in order to do it and we only had the one Division One professional league, so it didn't seem like the right time then and now GSL has come in as another Division One league and as they get the first couple of years under their belt, I feel like now we're going to also help grow amateur women's soccer in our country so it felt like the right time. Also, as we gear up for the World Cup in 2031, I think this is great timing in order to create another competition." As with the Open Cup, the Crest Cup winner will be able to qualify for the Concacaf W Champions Cup, broadening experiences for players and staff alike. "Most of the players and the coaches and the teams in our ecosystem, they only get that international exposure if they make their national teams or if they're lucky, one or two teams, to be able to play in the Concacaf tournament but this is another way to get more players interleague competition that could then lead to international competition in really meaningful games, right?" she said. "Because single elimination, you got to perform on the given day or you're eliminated and then hopefully around the corner, this leads to being able to play in the Women's Club World Cup." It is likely that Crest Cup games will take place midweek, in between the weekend games that usually take up the calendar in the NWSL and the GSL, but Parlow Cone said it was too early to say definitively. Finding spots on the schedule to play Crest Cup games will be among U.S. Soccer's biggest challenges since player load is changing at the highest levels of the game. In the last two years alone, the inaugural editions of the Concacaf W Champions Cup and the FIFA Women's Champions Cup have been staged, while FIFA also intends to introduce a Women's Club World Cup. The latter competition is reportedly slated to take place in the U.S. in the winter of 2028, according to the Guardian, only adding to the new types of games players might face. On the flip side, players outside the NWSL run the risk of playing too few games - the 2026 GSL season, for example, runs from August to November and will only feature 14 regular-season matches. Parlow Cone said she is working in collaboration with both the NWSL and the GSL to find the right spots on the calendar while taking player load into consideration. "I'm a former player so this is always top of mind for me specifically," she said. "I've said it several times. We could not be working more closely with NWSL and GSL and their sporting leaders to create models for the schedules for the exact reason that you mentioned and we want to make sure that we're not overloading the players, not underloading and allowing enough recovery between their league matches and the Crest Cup matches so like I said before, I would imagine that this would be mostly midweek matches but I'm not gonna declaratively say that right now. We're not announcing a launch date, I'm definitely not telling you what day of the week we're gonna play the matches quite yet."

news.title: Ashley Sanchez makes her case as USWNT battle back for draw against Spain
news.desc: Ashley Sanchez and Mallory Swanson scored to help the U.S. team claw their way out of a 2-0 deficit against the world champions
text: CHESTER, Pa. – The U.S. women's national team needed to start solidly against Spain on Tuesday, four days after the visitors took a two-goal lead in 14 minutes and never looked back. The steady start came but by the 32nd minute, the USWNT were in the same exact pickle. Two defensive lapses cost them against the reigning world champions and the USWNT were in need of a problem-solver with roughly an hour still left on the clock.
On a team that boasts several likely suspects, one finally emerged – Ashley Sanchez.
Ashley Sanchez scores in her first USWNT start in 714 days 💪 pic.twitter.com/gfHqyCJqIk

Sophia Wilson darted towards goal but with a defender inching closer, she sent the ball to her left. It slowly drifted towards Sanchez, who had the space to do whatever she wanted. She cut inside and entered the penalty area, unbothered by the two defenders in front of her who had otherwise proven to be up for the task of handling the U.S. team's historically capable offense. They left a crevice of space that only the most talented of players could exploit, Sanchez rising to the challenge effortlessly. The ball took a bounce near the goal line but she took the hit for a reason – no one was in a position to stop it and so it landed in the back of the net, just as she had intended.

The moment of brilliance is hardly a surprise from the NWSL's golden boot leader, the 27-year-old in the form of her life and as well-equipped as any to rattle an otherwise sturdy Spain back line. Sanchez had earned her spot in the starting lineup on Tuesday, the USWNT's most dynamic attacker a natural inclusion on a day they hoped to show the attacking end product that was missing in Saturday's loss. The overall results were mixed – the U.S. team still came out with a 2-2 draw, Spain the aggressors this time on a day where their attacking might was genuinely hard to miss. In Sanchez, though, the USWNT had a bright spot.

"Her experience, her maturity and the ability to be able to transfer knowledge," head coach Emma Hayes said post-match. "Even she said to me at the end, 'There's so much I still need to be able to do,' which is natural but I thought she did a great job. I'm really happy for her to get a goal."

Until Sanchez's goal, the USWNT had gone goalless in 139 minutes of play against Spain and not for a lack of effort. Finishing was an issue – they generated 2.26 expected goals without actually scoring, the issue exemplified in Lily Yohannes' missed penalty midway through the second half. Matters felt worse at halftime of Tuesday's defeat, the U.S. team only generating 0.23 expected goals from six shots. They were in desperate need of someone who would finally make a difference and Sanchez stepped up, both at a timely juncture for the team and for herself.

Sanchez had been out of the national team picture for two years until this month's friendlies, though her return had become undeniable by the time Hayes named the roster two weeks earlier. She had pulled off the feat after a position change at the North Carolina Courage, enjoying the best season of her career as a left winger after years of playing in midfield. Finding a way to impress against Spain would be another challenge entirely but one Sanchez ultimately embraced, making her case not a moment too soon.

"I think it felt natural, but obviously I think there's a little bit of, still, tactical adjustment that I need to have and because I haven't been here for that long," Sanchez said, reflecting on her first USWNT camp in two years. "It has only been a week. I know that I, defensively, could do a little bit better, so I think for me, that's my biggest takeaway. I'm really happy with the goal, but I think it did feel comfortable on the field with the connections that I have, but ultimately, I know I still have some [room for] improvement."

The Spain friendlies were always destined to test the USWNT's depth, especially without a few key players through injury, Sanchez adding to the narrative in all the right ways. She started in the place of Alyssa Thompson, who was amongst the positives on Saturday and still very much looks like a potential starter at the Women's World Cup in eight months' time. That spot on the left of Hayes' preferred three-person front line, though, is as competitive as any on a team that has aimed to have cover in just about every position on the pitch.

Hayes has a good type of problem on her hands in that position, if this week's games are anything to go by. How she picks between two talented players who seem poised to make a difference on good days and bad is one of the many questions that await over the next eight months, though in some ways it may not need answering. On days where the U.S. team's shortcomings are on display, particularly in defense without the injured Naomi Girma and Sam Coffey, that very specific type of depth might be the exact thing to bail Hayes' side out of trouble in a make-or-break situation.

Sanchez was hardly the only person to offer a reminder of the USWNT's historic dominance in attack. Mallory Swanson's 86th-minute equalizer marked her first goal for the national team since welcoming her daughter Josie nearly a year ago, the forward slowly working her way back into the group in just her second international game after maternity leave.

"I honestly thought Michelle [Cooper] was going to finish it, but the defender did well and recovered, and she made the right decision in the box, and I was just able to take a touch and come across my body and finish it."
Mallory Swanson scores her first USWNT goal since the Olympic gold medal match to bring them level 2-2 with Spain 😤 pic.twitter.com/4I4VC0oexv

It was vintage Swanson, her goal calling back to her crowning achievement thus far with the U.S. team. She played a central role in the gold medal run at the 2024 Olympics in Paris, scoring four goals, including the lone goal in the final against Brazil. In a week that was ultimately defined by the USWNT's inability to convert their chances, Swanson's goal was a welcome development for Hayes and company.

"I think Mal has shown improvement every day in training," Hayes said. "Didn't think she was quite ready for 45, so we did push, and I said to her, 'You've got another one in you at this level,' and she's in a better place to be able to perform more consistently, but I say it all the time -- she's an important player on our team, and I think the more we have her back, the better it'll get. I think she missed a big chance. It reminded me of the Olympic gold medal moment. I was like, 'This is the one player you want in this position,' and she lifted it, but she didn't miss the second one. That's what you have to do at this level, though. You don't get many. You got to finish them."

There is still time on the clock for the USWNT to fully flesh out their World Cup identity, while the job of actually qualifying for next summer's tournament in Brazil is technically still on the to-do list -- next month's Conccacf W Championship quarterfinal against El Salvador is essentially a win-and-in game. Hayes' embarrassment of riches in attack, though, might make up for the weaknesses in the back that were apparent over the course of both friendlies against Spain. Though the U.S. team played with a more traditional No. 6 in Claire Hutton on Tuesday, the defensive unit as a whole still succumbed to their opponent's attacking brilliance. The newness of the connections might be to blame, at least partially. Tierna Davidson and Kennedy Wesley only played their second game together at center back, while they had a different goalkeeper behind them this time in Phallon Tullis-Joyce.

"It's really important to be able to build a partnership, I think, especially as a center back partnership because it's not just like us having to do our jobs but it's a lot of us organizing forward," Davidson said. "To be able to kind of learn each other's tendencies and build that relationship is really important because I think going into tournaments, the strength of our team is our depth, so whatever combination of players that needs to be on the field for us to win, the more that you can have all of the relationships built, the better. So I think it's a really important thing for us to do in these types of games is to kind of be in those pressure moments and build, and honestly, sometimes it is making mistakes. Maybe it is we're not fully on the same page, but these are the moments to get that right."

Unseating Girma, arguably the game's best center back, is perhaps an unrealistic expectation for Wesley or anyone else technically in the running. By force or otherwise, though, Hayes continues to leave no stone unturned when it comes to actually handing players' experiences well before their major tournament debuts come around.

"We've got to develop a group and in one game, you're going to rely on one situation," Hayes said. "Another group, it might be another. The importance is the whole pack, especially in a game where you've got eight subs. At a World Cup, don't know what the sub pattern will be but the benches are critical. Gone are the days of an 11. That's finished in top flight football so I always wonder why people keep asking, 'What's the settled 11 going to be?' That's a story of the past in football. You're never going to always have your best players available because of whatever reason -- injury, form -- so you have to have enough who know how to play and the same with Spain. Spain still maximized eight subs. They've got a whole development system where they can slip one out, one in. Seamless. Doesn't matter if they're missing some of their best players. They demonstrated in two games why they're world champions so we have to get up to that level."

news.title: What to watch in UEFA Champions League: All eyes on Manchester City vs PSG; Real Madrid face big test at Roma
news.desc: Enzo Maresca's side faces the ultimate tactical test against back-to-back champions PSG, while Jose Mourinho brings Real Madrid to the Stadio Olimpico
text: Well Tuesday's games sure didn't disappoint. Saka got his scoring boots on in a 3-0 win for Arsenal over Lille, just like we told you he would, and Barcelona once again ran up the score, so we were 2-2 on that front. Though the real drama was in Manchester United entering yet another crisis with a 2-0 loss to Atletico Madrid and Bayern Munich drawing 3-3 with the Norwegian underdogs, Viking.
As for Wednesday's game, well there's only one place to start.

Almost the last aspect of Manchester City to find itself under the microscope over recent weeks has been the team here and now under Enzo Maresca's leadership and their ability to win games in the weeks ahead. One might argue that that is a fitting aspect of the suite of punishments that will be meted out unless they are successful in their appeal. City's 114 breaches of Premier League financial rules have warped both the English and European game for so long that the temptation for some might be just not to look.

That might work in the Premier League, where the prospect of points deductions or expulsion means that games like Sunday's 3-0 win at Liverpool might actually prove to have been irrelevant. The Champions League is rather different. UEFA struck out in their probe in 2020, the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturning a two-year Champions League ban as the alleged breaches were mostly either time-barred or not established.

Whatever City achieve in Europe this season is much more likely to count. The idea of this team playing in the EFL and UCL as holders next season ought not to be entirely discounted. Most bookmakers have them as fifth or sixth favorites, at worst somewhere just outside the inner circle of contenders. Opta gives only Arsenal a better chance of winning the competition.

The current Premier League table tells you they could achieve a great deal given they have won six of six to go with their win in Porto to start off the competition. It might not be entirely truthful at this early juncture. Pep Guardiola is due to return to the Etihad on Wednesday night to offer his support to the embattled club (and, based on his public statements, the ownership too). What he will see is a team that is so far yet to kick some of the bad habits that cost them titles in his final years.

In particular, this team looks vulnerable to being cut through on the counter for reasons that will be relatively obvious if you check their pass network in last month's 5-3 win over Sunderland. Enzo Maresca's system is written as a 4-2-3-1 but Enzo Fernandez (No.17 above) is as much an attacking midfielder at the Etihad as he was when these two were together at Chelsea. The Sunderland game is an extreme example of his positioning and that of No.10 Rayan Cherki, but this bears a few hallmarks of Guardiola's time with a 4-3-3 of free eights in Kevin De Bruyne and David Silva, both superior pressers to the current attacking midfielders. It is fair to say that even a toned-down version of this approach is contingent on Elliot Anderson (No.5) continuing to be as excellent as he has been early in his City career.

Certainly it might well look vulnerable if Paris Saint-Germain show up with their midfield at full strength. The relatively diffident approach the back-to-back champions take to the league phase is a reminder not to overindex any results that don't go their way. Equally, one could see Desire Doue flitting infield and/or Ousmane Dembele dropping off the front to overwhelm Anderson and create angles for runners from wide areas.

"We need the perfect performance because they are the best team in Europe," said Maresca of the task ahead of City. "They have won the past two Champions Leagues. We need the perfect game but, doing our best, I think we can beat them and be happy at the end." Whether anyone would be happy for them is quite another matter.
Date: Wednesday, Oct. 14 | Time: 3 p.m. ETLocation: Etihad Stadium -- Manchester, United KingdomLive stream: Paramount+Odds: Man City +115; Draw +280; PSG +190

Jose Mourinho will probably relish the welcome the Stadio Olimpico affords him on his return to the side he led to the Conference League. When the ball gets rolling? Perhaps not so much. His Real Madrid side are of course favorites given the sheer weight of talent they can roll onto the field -- enough to down Inter in their Champions League opener -- but while Mourinho still puzzles out the right system to nullify the issues with the left-leaning attack, he is running into an opponent that knows exactly who they are. And Roma will be changing for no one.

"Our attitude led us to play these types of matches and finish third last year," head coach Gianpiero Gasperini said. "We have characteristics we don't change. We know Real's value, but they aren't the first valuable team we meet. It doesn't take them much to create dangerous situations, but that's part of what makes great teams great. I don't think Roma's characteristics should be distorted."

That Gasperini went on to suggest Wednesday's opponents have "room for improvement" "in terms of the aesthetic quality of their football" seemed less like a dig from a rival coach and more an expert assessment. Few coaches are as adept as Gasperini at getting their team to hum in possession, whose Roma outfit rank seventh in Europe's top five leagues in terms of non-penalty expected goals per game.

The talent is impressive but not remarkably so, the closest Roma have to a star being Paulo Dybala defying age curves in the Eternal City. Meanwhile, players have started over 30 Serie A games since the start of last season, a number that would surely be higher if Dybala were always fit. Across the pitch there are groupings that just seem to click, most notably the steadying Bryan Cristante offering a platform for Manu Kone to excel in midfield. The rich run of form that propelled this side into the Champions League at the back end of last season and the title race early in this is a triumph of the collective.

Well, that and a bit of coaching stardust. Since arriving in Italy in January, Donyell Malen has 24 Serie A goals. Across Europe's top five leagues, only five players beat that mark. The evidence of Gasperini's time at Atalanta suggests this is less a matter of Roma unlocking superstar talent, more that their coach can turn ordinary forwards into world beaters.

In a 3-5-2 system with fearless wing backs, Roma look like a team that could give Real Madrid plenty of issues in the likely event that Kylian Mbappe and Vinicius Junior leave the out-of-possession stuff to the rest of their side. Now, of course, those players could puncture the bubble of their fearless hosts with just a couple of chances. Gasperini, though, has every reason to back the courage of his convictions. This is a team that could deliver quite an upset.
Date: Wednesday, Oct. 14 | Time: 3 p.m. ETLocation: Stadio Olimpico -- RomeLive stream: Paramount+Odds: Roma +250; Draw +280; Real Madrid -118

A disastrous 2025-26 season for Chelsea meant that Stamford Bridge might have stood empty for much of the winter. Happily for Shakhtar Donetsk, that is not the case, the Ukrainian champions are playing the first of their four home league phase games against AEK Athens in west London. The ties that Mykhailo Mudryk's transfer forged between the Premier League giants and Shakhtar, without a home since 2014 and unable to host European games in Ukraine since the invasion of Russia, remain strong, such that Blues owner Behdad Eghbali was only too ready to lend his stadium out.

You can read more about how Shakhtar and their ownership plan to use their London visits to draw investment in Ukraine here, but there is also the football to consider. The Ukrainian champions gave an impressive account of themselves in drawing at PSV Eindhoven in their first game, all the more so given that an XI with an average age of 24 is the youngest in the competition so far. It may be that they do not have long left with head coach Arda Turan, the subject of several links with the vacant Turkey job, and that increases the importance of this game. A win at their new home and Shakhtar would be well set for a first knockout berth since 2014-15.
Date: Wednesday, Oct. 14 | Time: 3 p.m. ETLocation: Stamford Bridge -- LondonLive stream: Paramount+Odds: Shakhtar Donetsk +160; Draw +225; AEK Athens +163

news.title: USWNT's 2-2 draw with Spain maps the work that's ahead of the 2027 World Cup for hungry USA soccer
news.desc: The Americans proved that they can compete with the best team in the world, but there is work to do
text: CHESTER, Pa. - From the moment the first ball was kicked, it felt like a game with high stakes between the United States and Spain as titans of the game clashed. In total, 18,648 fans in Chester cheered every clearance, tackle, and promising attack at the top of their lungs until, and as she does to many a team around the world, Alexia Putellas took the air out of the stadium by splitting the USWNT central defense, but they were able to show resilience as Mallory Swanson drew level in the 86th minute of play for a 2-2 draw.

As the road to the 2027 World Cup becomes clearer by the day, one thing is evident. Spain are the team to beat, as no matter who Sonia Bermudez puts in the lineup, Spain will be compact in defense and pull you out of position to finish their own chances. This is a spot the USWNT used to be in, but as Hayes figures out her best XI on the fly while missing key players like Naomi Girma, who was supposed to be in this camp before picking up an injury with Chelsea, there's a way to go in order to defeat the number one team in the world. And that's a fact that Hayes is aware of.
"They're the best team in the world. I didn't learn anything that I didn't already know," Hayes said when asked what she learned during this camp.

While it's not to state that the gap is larger than it is between these teams, it drives home the point that the USWNT now play in a world where they aren't the favorites; they are among the favorites, but it's the little moments that determine how those top sides in the world shake out.

While it seemed like Emily Fox was setting a physical tone early in the match, that bite didn't last, and ball watching helped gift the second goal of the game. On the bright side, part of the path to how the USWNT can get ready for these moments also showcased itself in the same match via Ashley Sanchez. Taking on two Spanish defenders, the N.C. Courage winger was able to secure a great finish in the second half, notching her first start since October of 2024 with a memorable moment.
Ashley's first goal since 2022 🦅USWNT x @vw pic.twitter.com/xRuNztkgE5

You'd want Sanchez's goal to come at a time when the USWNT are level with Spain versus already trailing, but that's the gap that Hayes is looking to close. On their day, this team can defeat anyone in the world; the Olympics have proven that, but now they have to add consistency, which has been lacking during this camp. Being able to fight back is an important quality, and getting Swanson back to her best will be critical for the team to get where they want to be. In only six matches in Paris, Swanson scored four goals and assisted two more, and while the attack is deep, she's a game changer.

It's great to see someone confident in their finishes, and Sanchez was just that, cutting in from the left wing. Most days she'll generate more than .17 xG, but also, if that's all that she needs to score, the USWNT will benefit from it.
These were also meaningful goals for their teammates to see too.

"I'm so pumped for them. Sanchez is back for the first time in a bit, and I think she earned that goal. She's been playing so incredibly for her club, and I think she capitalized on the opportunities that she was given, and she did great," Rose Lavelle said. "I think for Mal, coming back from having a baby is no easy feat at all, and she does it with such grace, and I'm just happy for them both. And for the team to have two players who can come into a game like this and do that is incredible for us."

Teams like Spain exposing flaws is a good thing since it gives Hayes and the squad things to fine-tune when they get together again in November for the Concacaf W Championship facing El Salvador, when they won't have a long layoff between camps like they did between facing Brazil in June and now in October. That makes it easier for Hayes to continue building relationships because the structure is there as they enter the competition that serves as World Cup qualifying.

Alyssa Thompson echoed how important it is to play in these games, not only so that they can be challenges for the players who have been to major tournaments, but for those trying to make their first, it's a great chance to measure yourself against the best in the world and see where you need to grow.

Only time will improve how passes between the squad find each other, and knowing when to shoot or take on their defenders. There's also the bright spot of Kate Del Fava getting an assist on her USWNT debut, which is yet another thing to build. Hayes has now used 46 players this year with the USWNT, which is a new record as she ensures she sees what she has in each of them. When a new player makes a debut like Del Fava today, the team is also undefeated, which is an excellent sign when looking to find these combinations.

It's all about Hayes putting her Legos in the right configuration because this team can beat Spain, and to win the World Cup, they may need to, and they'll just need to configure the pieces in the right order. And when you want a tactician to lead the ship, there's no one that the USWNT would rather have at the helm than Hayes to set the squad up, building off of these friendlies for what they hope will be a run to the World Cup final.

news.title: Lisandro Martinez just said what every Man United fan is thinking after embarrassing UCL loss at Atletico
news.desc: United lost 2-0 at Atletico Madrid on Tuesday, and their Argentine defender did not hold back as their horrible start to the season continues
text: Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez did not hold back on his team after Tuesday's 2-0 defeat at Atletico Madrid, arguing the Red Devils' squad is not strong enough to compete in Europe's top club competition.

United conceded in the first minute thanks to a goal from Alex Baena, while Ademola Lookman bagged a second in the 79th minute of a dominant performance from the Spanish side. The result leaves United with just three wins in nine games across all competitions this season, which is Michael Carrick's first full campaign as the head coach after taking over the role last winter.

"We're not playing well as a team," Martinez said on the UEFA Champions League Today post-match show. "You can see the disconnection. We can't [string] three or four passes together, and the body language [is bad]. We missed some chances, we are negative, and yeah, when you play against these teams, especially in Champions League, you can't miss opportunities and you can't concede the goal we conceded in the first minutes."
Martinez used the opportunity to push for higher standards, arguing that United are capable of more than their record suggests.

"Trying to be positive and trying to be honest," he added. "We have to change, to do more. Because we are capable to do better. We have the players. But also, when you watch television and watch the games, you see the players and the managers and you put the finger [and blame them], which is right. We take the responsibility, but also as a club, I expect more. I'm not gonna close my mouth. I expect more. We need more ambition. We need to talk more about winning Champions League, talk more about winning the Premier League instead of other things."

Martinez, who joined the Red Devils in the summer of 2022, also reflected on the fact that the team has been in a period of inconsistency for the entirety of his time with the club. United's ups and downs, though, stretch back more than a decade; they last won the Premier League title in the 2012-13 in what was Sir Alex Ferguson's final season in charge, his shadow looming large since.
"Every season, we're talking about the same thing," Martinez said. "Of course, but if we don't say the truth, nothing will change."
Atleti manager Diego Simeone was also critical of United's approach over the course of the game, one that ultimately suited his side just fine despite the surprise.

"We knew what they were going to do," Simeone told the UEFA Champions League Today post-match show. "We needed to find the opposite side from where they started their press ... we knew we could find success there. In the first half, we would press their right flank a lot of the times and Baena or Grimaldo would find that space behind to launch an attack and start an important transition like we had in various opportunities. We knew that if we beat their press, we would find ourselves with tons of space to run, like we did with the first goal"
Martinez repeated his sentiments in different post-match broadcast interviews over the course of the evening, hitting a particularly harsh note in his discussion with Amazon Prime.

"Really poor," he said. "Really poor. I have to control myself a lot but sometimes is a reflection of the mirror of how is our club at the moment. We did a fantastic season last season and now we expect more from the top, more players to compete because many teams bring many players as well. Atletico have an amazing team and they deserve to win today. I expect more [investment]. 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]. I have to be honest, as players we have to do more but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night."

news.title: Champions League expert picks, predictions, best bets: Can Man City top PSG in high-pressure return to Etihad?
news.desc: Check out all the picks from our experts as the Champions League league phase rolls on
text: The Champions League is finally back. Five weeks after an opening matchday that delivered goals aplenty, Europe's elite return to the league phase on Tuesday and Wednesday, and the Matchday 2 slate wastes no time getting serious. Wednesday's headliner comes at the Etihad, where Manchester City host Paris Saint-Germain in what is City's first UCL game since they were found guilty of 114 financial charges. Their first game since the charges was actually on Sunday at Liverpool, and that went more than well.

Real Madrid, 2-1 winners over Inter in their opener, head to Rome with their former coach Jose Mourinho already fuming, while many giants are on upset alert with some intriguing away clashes, including Barcelona's visit to Istanbul to take on Galatasaray.
Then there's Como. The Serie A side stunned RB Leipzig 4-1 in their first-ever Champions League match and now visit Feyenoord looking to prove that night was no fluke.

Every match streams live on Paramount+, your home for every Champions League game all season long, plus replays, highlights and studio coverage breaking down the race for the top eight. If you haven't signed up yet, now's the time.

Person to watch: Pep Guardiola, N.A. -- When news of Manchester City having committed 114 breaches of Premier League rules arrived over the international break, many wondered how Pep Guardiola, their manager of a decade before leaving in the summer, might react. After all, he had previously said he would walk out of the club if he found out they had lied to him over their skirting of financial rules. Instead, Guardiola has rallied behind his former club in remarkable fashion, offering public support to the ownership. He is due to go one step further on Wednesday night, showing up at City's first home game since the verdict. Up in the Etihad stands, all eyes will be on Guardiola. Will he be able to avoid the temptation for some tactical tinkering? -- James Benge

Man of the match: Kvicha Kvaratskhelia -- PSG: The Georgian winger only scored one goal so far in the opening six Ligue 1 games and he's expected to react in the coming weeks, as he's been a key player for Luis Henrique and PSG over the past two years since he joined from Napoli. He left his mark in the two Champions League finals won by the French giants in the past two seasons and he's also a serious candidate for the 2026 Ballon d'Or. -- Francesco Porzio

Prediction: Manchester City 2, Paris Saint-Germain 2 -- This match is brought to you by sovereign wealth funds, ones who have a well-documented ability to build superteams that can headline Champions League games, no matter the controversy. Manchester City's win over Liverpool on Sunday proved that the team are doing what they can: somehow focus on the games in front of them despite the possibility of serious penalties for financial breaches of epic proportions, so much so that they will be hard to count out against Paris Saint-Germain. Whether or not the result feels tainted, though, is another question entirely. -- Pardeep Cattry

Best bet: Erling Haaland to have 2+ shots on target (-140) -- There are plenty of reasons off the pitch to keep an eye on City's return to their home stadium but if anyone can rise above and keep producing, it's Haaland. He was able to score to silence the Anfield crowd and while goals will be hard to come by in this game, he'll have his chances to test the keeper for shots on target during this clash. -- Charles Booth

news.title: Arsenal's rotated squad weren't up to par, but Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard's substitutions changed the game
news.desc: Arsenal were ultimately too much for Lille as the lineup changes showed that sometimes depth just means giving your stars an hour off
text: LONDON -- Depth is nice, especially when you have as much of it as Arsenal, two deep in every position, able to shade an injury at left back by simply shunting their England international center midfielder into the other position where he has excelled against some of the best in the world.

Ultimately, though Mikel Arteta can be bequeathed as many options as Andrea Berta can rustle up, there's no way that you are not going to feel the absence of a fit and in-form Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard. That much was clear as Lille became the latest side to be overwhelmed by what Arteta likes to term his finishers, a role that his substitutes certainly lived up to in the final 25 minutes at the Emirates Stadium.

The breakthrough had just come when Arteta deployed Saka, Odegaard and Kai Havertz, a clipped finish by Jurrien Timber bringing relief to an antsy ground that had seen too many promising attacks die just outside the penalty area. Arsenal had been too slow, too desynchronised, too often in each other's way. It said everything about the quartet that had started the game that right back Timber looked as likely to get a goal as any of them.

Noni Madueke was very capable of getting the ball into good positions, less effective when he got there. Mikel Merino deployed the skill that makes him so impactful as a substitute -- a patient assessment of his options before picking the right one -- to slow down attacks. Eberechi Eze ran into blind alleys. Viktor Gyokeres? Well it was another game without a shot for the Swede, whose 1.9 penalty box touches per 90 is less than half those of Timber. The only players who average fewer are center backs, defensive midfielders and goalkeepers.

Bruno Guimaraes tried to win it himself and occasionally looked like he might, denied a penalty early in the second half and spurning the best chance of the first half when he diverted Timber's cutback just wide of the near post. The Brazilian aside this was leaden-footed stuff, at least until those substitutes added some levity to proceedings. The first attack after the changes and Arsenal drove through the gears, Odegaard and Guimaraes combining to find Saka down the right. His first-time cross off his nominally weaker right foot found Eze in stride to stroke home.

Here were the stars making the fringe guys look even better. In the 20 minutes after the triple change, Eze took three shots, one more than he had in the preceding 65. The space he had had to craft for himself beforehand was now there for Arsenal's No.10 to exploit, the service impeccable.

A third came when the big three of Arsenal's attack combined themselves: Odegaard, Saka, Odegaard again through to Havertz, who rolled the ball across for Saka to finish. It is now eight games in all competitions for Saka with a big chance, double his previous best. His finishing might have been wayward before today, but having an elite progressor and creator getting into so many scoring positions augurs incredibly well for Arsenal.

So does what Arteta got from several of his fringe attackers tonight. While the abiding takeaway is that Arsenal's best attackers are better than the rest, it is worth noting that with Madueke, Merino and Eze leading the way, this team was still good enough to hold a Champions League opponent at arms' length, and that Madueke himself did eventually get an assist. This wasn't the rescue job that Guimaraes drove against Leeds, instead it was Arteta's best players getting half an hour-ish to overwhelm an opponent who had been ground down, even as Arsenal struggled in the final third. Saka and company really only needed five minutes.

news.title: Three keys for USWNT to bounce back against Spain at Subaru Park in rematch against defending World Cup champs
news.desc: Emma Hayes wants her squad to capitalize on its chances after generating 10 shots on target without a goal in Saturday's 2-0 defeat
text: The United States women's national team will get one more chance to prove they're among the world's best on Tuesday night at Subaru Park. The group will try to bounce back against Spain and close out the international window after Saturday's 2-0 loss, in which Spain took the lead just 14 minutes in. Despite a flurry of shot creation and attempts on goal, the squad couldn't escape the early hole it dug itself into. The questions facing the team and head coach Emma Hayes are as much about adjustments as they are about finishing in the final third. Here are three keys to the upcoming game:
Date: Tuesday, Oct. 13 | Time: 7 p.m. ETLocation: Subaru Park -- Chester, Pa.TV: TNT | Live stream: HBO MaxOdds: USWNT +165; Draw +230; Spain +140

The biggest stat Hayes has emphasized following the loss is the team's high totals in shot creation and attempts on target, with nothing to show for it. She's been clear in press conferences that "you can't give them a head start" when discussing the two goals conceded in the first friendly, but the group's response was the highlight despite the lack of goals. "We have to tighten up on those things because actually, they didn't create a lot of chances, and I think if we defend those moments better, it at least puts us into a stronger position. But I think once you go two nil down against them, then you are faced with chasing the game. And I think probably the first 30 minutes did fine; 30 to 45 minutes, I think we lost our structure. I think the second half it was all about us, but you also have to score to win games," Hayes said in pregame comments. Despite going down 2-0 early, the squad rallied in attack and finished with 13 shots, 10 on target, and 2.26 expected goals to Spain's 0.43. Hayes sees those numbers as a positive for now. "But I'm not worried about it. I think this is part of the process. As I said, if I'm here to merely protect a wins record, then I'll pick a lesser opponent. But I'm not here to do that. I'm here to see, well, how much does that gap close with them? And then how far away are we from that, and keep working towards it because they're the best team in the world for a reason," Hayes said.

The last time the USWNT got together was the June window. They played two friendlies against Brazil in the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup host nation. It was a taste of what a potential future tournament environment could look like, and they lost the opening match to Brazil 2-1. It's been four months since the group last came together, and some are in the mix for the first time or after long absences. "We've had one classroom session, and then we trained with the group that hadn't played in any of the minutes. So, as a team, we get our first opportunity now to do those things. I think it's always about doing the same things regardless of result, we've done a game review around the things that we can identify as really clear patterns that we break. Is as it is every game of football, you play the same opponent twice, and there's things within that you can do a bit better," Hayes said of the team's two days since the loss. As in previous fixtures against top opponents this year, Hayes expects a response from the players in the second game. "And I think our team has a really good habit of bringing them things into the second game, but we have to do them. Like I say this many times, you can get away with things against weaker opposition. You just can't with [Spain], and so I'll be looking for us to apply that detail to what we're doing, but also know that you don't really have much of a turn turnaround," Hayes said. Patri Guijarro's opening goal on Saturday showed how quickly Spain turn space into a chance. La Roja recorded only three shots on target but scored twice, so the USWNT cannot afford to be generous around the central areas in front of their back line. Quick pressure on the first pass into Spain's midfield may help limit their most typical route to goal.

All this is to say that the USWNT wouldn't typically find themselves in a compact shape between the lines, but they were dangerous in transition. That threat can disrupt some of Spain's discipline in their switches and movement with the ball, though it may all be easier said than done when you consider the opponent and timing of the window. "Some players are coming to the back end of the season. Some are at the beginning of their season. We've been four or five months apart. We're only together nine days. We have two training sessions, one game. I think sometimes we think, 'God, everything must look a certain way. It's got to look completely perfect,' and actually, it's quite clunky that first game," Hayes said. "I'm expecting it to be a little bit better for us, much like it was when we played Brazil Game Two, or we played Japan with the same group game one and three. I think my big request to the team is start earlier. Like start earlier with the things that really matter, and that's what I'll be encouraging us to do [Tuesday]."

news.title: Emma Hayes works to break club habits on a short schedule as USWNT prepares for Spain rematch
news.desc: After a 2-0 defeat on Saturday, Emma Hayes is using another test against the world champions to fix attacking chemistry and integrate Ashley Sanchez
text: CHESTER, Pa. - International soccer can be a puzzle. Players fly in from various clubs, you get a limited amount of time together, and then there's the expectation to go out and defeat some of the best teams in the world. That's the kind of puzzle that Emma Hayes has been brought in to solve, which she has done by pushing the United States women's national team to win the Olympics in 2024. Now she's once again looking to set her side up to defeat reigning world champions Spain.

These are the kind of matches that Hayes wants, as she invited the pressure in her pre-match press conference, saying, "If I'm here to merely protect a win's record, then I'll pick a lesser opponent."
Date: Tuesday, Oct. 13 | Time: 7 p.m. ETLocation: Subaru Park -- Chester, Pa.TV: TNT | Live stream: HBO MaxOdds: USWNT +165; Draw +230; Spain +140

It's a match that feels like a tournament scenario, with only one day of training in between, but the team did have time to review video to make the adjustments needed after Saturday's 2-0 loss to Spain. From passing when players should shoot to a lack of cohesion in attack, the time apart showed for a squad that was last together in June to face Brazil. Hayes wants to ensure her players are ready for the demands of national team soccer, which has a different flavor from club soccer.

"This window I always think's quite tricky when you've been apart for five months as well. Cause it's, they come in with habits from their club, and then, oh we've got to break them habits in two sessions," Hayes said. "And so if you're in your club, for example, largely player-for-player, and here we're largely zonal, that's really hard for players. Cause even the new players say, you know what, it's really difficult. I'm so used to marking a player in every situation. And at the international level you, neither play zonal and as well as player to player. So sometimes it takes a little bit of time to get into that. It's far from ideal when you've had four or five months apart."

Hayes then went on to discuss some of those differences, including how they impact Ashley Sanchez. While this is the first time that Hayes has called in Sanchez during her tenure, the North Carolina Courage winger has been thriving in the NWSL, where she has 20 goals this season. In club play, Sanchez doesn't have to track back much, but with the national team, that's something Hayes wants to see, and Sanchez has been working on it.

The need for a second finisher alongside Sophia Wilson was clear in the first match against Spain, and while Sanchez, off the bench, got a chance that she wasn't able to convert, she's someone who, if club form translates to the national team, will make this team a well-oiled machine. So far, the signs are good, as Hayes is happy with what she's seeing.

"I've been impressed with her all week," Hayes said. "I've been impressed with her character and, um, how easily she settled into the group and I'm happy for her because I do think we need these experienced players to step up where there's a big gap between our real senior and real less experienced players. I think the team really needs an Ashley Sanchez to step forward and provide a little more competition."

Considering that Sanchez has generally played as a No. 9 or No. 10 during her career, this quick progression is impressive in itself. There's a balance to be struck in national team camp. Some of what players do as the stars of their club teams still applies, but they also need a level of trust in their teammates to take their own chances, as Wilson notes. Following the first Spain match, Hayes noted that she wanted to see more hold-up play from Wilson to get teammates into the mix.

"It's trusting the players around you, knowing that everyone's doing their job," Wilson said. "And I think for me, it's the relationships. Obviously, there are different players that I'm playing with here and at club, and it's knowing your teammates and knowing what they're going to do at any given moment and their tendencies, and vice versa, and I'm understanding what I'm gonna do, and I think just figuring that out quickly is what you have to do with this team and in the time that we have."

This is where the work-in-progress nature of the team begins to show. Not only is Hayes without players who have been regulars in the team, but players are still figuring out those relationships alongside each other while playing tough matches. These are reps that will pay off, though. Few teams in the world can give the United States the level of challenge that Spain have, and they'll be better for experiencing it.

These issues will also get ironed out with time and a proper camp in tournament play. While there were four months between the last camp and this one, there will only be about a month between this camp coming to a close and facing El Salvador in the Concacaf W Championship in November. That will be a time to continue laying the foundation for a team that will be a serious contender for a World Cup crown. Hayes emphasizes doing the little things to be a cohesive unit and has also been building up the depth of the squad in order to have multiple avenues to success.

Seeing the changes from game one against Spain to game two will be one test, but so will seeing what these players retain in November as more players come back consistently. As long as health holds, it will be the third consecutive camp for Wilson. Mallory Swanson, will also be back in the fold for more time, and Sanchez, should she stay with the team will be aware of the expectations of a Hayes camp. It isn't always pretty looking at the guts of a squad as Hayes tinkers, but when it all comes together, her teams win, and this is a team learning to win under its coach.

news.title: Champions League expert picks, predictions, best bets: Man United face stiff test at Atletico
news.desc: Check out all the picks from our experts as the Champions League league phase rolls on
text: The Champions League is finally back. Five weeks after an opening matchday that delivered goals aplenty, Europe's elite return to the league phase on Tuesday and Wednesday, and the Matchday 2 slate wastes no time getting serious. Wednesday's headliner comes at the Etihad, where Manchester City host Paris Saint-Germain in what is City's first UCL game since they were found guilty of 114 financial charges. Their first game since the charges was actually on Sunday at Liverpool, and that went more than well.

Real Madrid, 2-1 winners over Inter in their opener, head to Rome with their former coach Jose Mourinho already fuming, while many giants are on upset alert with some intriguing away clashes, including Barcelona's visit to Istanbul to take on Galatasaray.

Then there's Como. The Serie A side stunned RB Leipzig 4-1 in their first-ever Champions League match and now visit Feyenoord looking to prove that night was no fluke. Arsenal, meanwhile, host Lille after grinding out a 1-0 win at Napoli.
In a league phase where every point counts, there's little room for a slow start.

Every match streams live on Paramount+, your home for every Champions League game all season long, plus replays, highlights and studio coverage breaking down the race for the top eight. If you haven't signed up yet, now's the time.

Player to watch: Alex Baena, Atletico Madrid -- Nine games into the season, World Cup winner Baena has already doubled his goal tally from year one at Atletico Madrid, and with 18 shots to his name, this is not a player who is afraid to pull the trigger. Nominally Atleti's left winger, Baena is free to switch flanks, step infield and just go where the move seems to take him. That might not sound very Diego Simeone-esque but when you have a talent like this on your hands, you make adjustments. -- James BengeMan of the match: Giuliano Simeone - Atletico Madrid -- The Argentinian winger had a strong start to the new season with two goals scored and two assists delivered so far in all competitions and he's now one of the key players of the team led by his father Diego. Giuliano is expected to be a pivotal player on Tuesday as well when Atletico Madrid will host Manchester United at the Metropolitano. -- Francesco Porzio

Prediction: Atletico Madrid 2, Manchester United 2 -- The question heading into this one is whether or not Manchester United can break out of their midtable Premier League mode to string together a dominant performance against a European perennial and ... the answer might be no. United might be better than their domestic record suggests but they struggle to get out of trouble and seem destined for a deadlock with last season's semifinalists, who have their own up-and-down track record in the Champions League. -- Pardeep Cattry

Best bet: Atletico Madrid to win (-110) -- It's all going wrong for Manchester United as even playing up a man they weren't able to get past Tottenham during the weekend and now the Red Devils face another tough test in Atletico Madrid away from home. Following their UCL win over Sabah, United have now failed to win in four consecutive matches while Michael Carrick's seat has to be getting warmer, and a loss in Madrid will continue a slide that he can't come back from. -- Charles Booth

Person to watch: Pep Guardiola, N.A. -- When news of Manchester City having committed 114 breaches of Premier League rules arrived over the international break, many wondered how Pep Guardiola, their manager of a decade before leaving in the summer might react. After all, he had previously said he would walk out of the club if he found out they had lied to him over their skirting of financial rules. Instead, Guardiola has rallied behind his former club in remarkable fashion, offering public support to the ownership. He is due to go one step further on Wednesday night, showing up at City's first home game since the verdict. Up in the Etihad stands, all eyes will be on Guardiola. Will he be able to avoid the temptation for some tactical tinkering? -- James Benge

Man of the match: Kvicha Kvaratskhelia -- PSG: The Georgian winger only scored one goal so far in the opening six Ligue 1 games and he's expected to react in the coming weeks, as he's been a key player for Luis Henrique and PSG over the past two years since he joined from Napoli. He left his mark in the two Champions League finals won by the French giants in the past two seasons and he's also a serious candidate for the 2026 Ballon d'Or. -- Francesco Porzio

Prediction: Manchester City 2, Paris Saint-Germain 2 -- This match is brought to you by sovereign wealth funds, ones who have a well-documented ability to build superteams that can headline Champions League games, no matter the controversy. Manchester City's win over Liverpool on Sunday proved that the team are doing what they can: somehow focus on the games in front of them despite the possibility of serious penalties for financial breaches of epic proportions, so much so that they will be hard to count out against Paris Saint-Germain. Whether or not the result feels tainted, though, is another question entirely. -- Pardeep Cattry

Best bet: Erling Haaland to have 2+ shots on target (-140) -- There are plenty of reasons off the pitch to keep an eye on City's return to their home stadium but if anyone can rise above and keep producing, it's Haaland. He's was able to score to silence the Anfield crowd and while goals will be hard to come by in this game, he'll have his chances to test the keeper for shots on target during this clash. -- Charles Booth

news.title: On night of mayhem for Liverpool, Barcola arrives in style
news.desc: Bradley Barcola's form was the subject of pre-match questions before Liverpool faced LASK. The French forward's Champions League hat-trick was the perfect answer.
text: On the eve of Liverpool's meeting with LASK, manager Andoni Iraola was repeatedly asked about the fortunes of Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola.

Given their price tags, the pressure was on both to start delivering after stuttering starts to their individual campaigns. Iraola, as most managers would, stood by his players, insisting he trusted them "100%".

Iraola insisted the focus was on the collective rather than individual stats but there is no denying that when you spend such eye-watering sums - £116m on Wirtz and £123m on Barcola - you want those players to be match-winners.
Wirtz delivered a fine display in the Austrian city of Linz as Liverpool won 6-3, with an assist to show for his efforts.
However, this was a night where the headlines belonged to Barcola, who on the 238th appearance of his career across clubs and country combined, scored his first hat-trick.
And it was those three goals which proved to be the difference as Liverpool returned to winning ways after their 3-0 loss to Manchester City on Sunday.

In truth, the 24-year-old could have scored more such was his quality, but he did enough to take the match ball home after two fine finishes with his right foot and left foot, followed by a tap in after the break.
And a little over 24 hours after defending his players against those pre-match questions, Iraola was speaking with a smile on his face.
"You were asking me yesterday about him not making the numbers and [the same with] Florian and I think both of them today played really, really well. I think they made a difference.
"Bradley was a threat, always when one-on-one [and] certainly in behind. He helped us a lot to control the game, finding the pockets. I am and happy for both of them.
"I think for their confidence it's very good. I think they feel now that we trust them a lot. I think it's going to be very good, very good for them."
On what it could mean for Barcola, Iraola added: "I think he has to enjoy this [as] to score a hat-trick in the Champions League is always very difficult.
"Even yesterday in training, I could feel he was very lively. Sometimes you feel these things [are going to happen]. We were feeling he was in a good place going into the game."
Barcola will now hope to show that level in the Premier League, starting with a visit to Brentford on Saturday.
Iraola's side were relentless in the first-half against the Austrian Bundesliga champions, racing into a three-goal lead. Such was their dominance, they could have easily scored more.
The 19 shots Liverpool had by half time against LASK was the most on record since 2003-04 by any team in the first half of a Champions League away match.
If there was any criticism, it would be that they were guilty of becoming a little complacent in the second half, conceding three goals after the hour mark but in fairness, the job was all but done.

There were more positives to take on the night, with both full-backs coming into the side and performing well. Jeremie Frimpong scored and registered two assists while Kostas Tsimikas added two assists of his own.
Ronald Araujo also scored his first goal for the club since joining in the summer and Lewis Koumas got no less than he deserved when he got on the scoresheet in the second half.

The 21-year-old even had two goals ruled out for offside but his first-half assist for Barcola meant that he became the youngster player to score and assist in a Champions League match for Liverpool (21y 25d), with the previous youngest being Steven Gerrard (21y 139d v Dynamo Kyiv in 2001). Fine company, indeed.
But Liverpool will know that they won’t get many easier games than this over the course of the season. LASK came into this game, winless in their last four matches.
“What do you take from that? It's very difficult because the game was very passive for large periods,” said Stephen Warnock on 5 Live.
”There were parts where I am watching Trey Nyoni in midfield and he has literally got no pressure on him at all, he is picking passes off.
“Barcola has got the run of his full-back who was taken off at half-time, which tells you everything.
“I don't read too much into it, because I expected Liverpool to go there and win, and win comfortably."
Warnock added that a bigger test for Liverpool will come at Brentford on Saturday, the Bees fourth in the table and unbeaten in the league.
“Can Barcola do that again, away at Brentford, because that is what they have essentially bought him for, to play in big games away from home," Warnock said.
“He hasn't played that much football this season so [this game] was about getting minutes in his legs and getting him fit and getting him sharper. The acid test will be Brentford away.”

news.title: Wilcox the target again in another damaging Man Utd fallout
news.desc: Lisandro Martinez's explosive comments after Manchester United's Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid turn the spotlight back on director of football Jason Wilcox.
text: It is almost 10 months since Jason Wilcox was in the line of fire when Ruben Amorim gave the explosive post-match news conference at Leeds that triggered his dismissal.
Amorim was furious Manchester United's director of football had subtly advised him to change tactics for the previous game against Wolves.
"I will do my job and every department, the scouting department, the sporting director, needs to do theirs," said Amorim.
Less than 24 hours after that chiding, Amorim was sacked, and the focus was on the part Wilcox played in that.
This time Lisandro Martinez was doing the firing and had a target in mind.
He might have got the job title slightly wrong, but there was no doubting who Martinez meant after the 2-0 loss to Atletico Madrid when he said: "I expect more from our technical director."
There is no doubting either that Martinez knew what he was saying.

Working as a post-match interviewer for US broadcaster CBS, legendary former United goalkeeper Peter Schmeichel tried to steer Martinez away from discussion about his old club's summer transfer window on four occasions. Each time, the Argentina defender refused to be deflected.
"We don't have the best squad at the moment compared to other top teams," said Martinez.
"I'm not going to close my mouth. We need more ambition. If we don't say the truth, nothing will change."

During the summer, BBC Sport was told by dressing room sources the club needed to sign more players than the three - Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans, Carlos Baleba - who eventually arrived, and it was "fairly obvious" where they needed to be - left-back and striker.
Another source with extensive knowledge of the inner workings at Old Trafford describes the current situation as "a mess".
Quiz: Do you remember the big names who took aim at football club chiefs?

Martinez said he felt it was important to speak out the way he did. Many United fans are delighted he went down that path, and the defender was highlighting inadequacies in the club's leadership structure.
The first is that Martinez's contract expires at the end of the season. United have the option to extend it by another year.

By being so outspoken against senior figures at the club, was he trying to ensure that option is not triggered, which would allow him to leave for nothing in the summer, or, potentially, for a lower fee in January?

Martinez is good friends with Atletico Madrid defender Cristian Romero and the international colleagues spoke after last night's game. Romero was similarly forceful against the Tottenham hierarchy last season.
Also, while the vast majority of United fans may agree with Martinez, internally his comments create a problem.

Most obviously, head coach Michael Carrick, having deflected questions about the defender's outburst in the immediate aftermath of the game, will face more probing on the matter when he speaks to the media before Sunday's trip to Leeds.

Any players lined up to talk around the Elland Road trip will be similarly quizzed. When Tielemans was asked about it by Amazon Prime on Tuesday night, he replied with a "no comment". Given the comments about recruitment, he would clearly be within his rights to ask Martinez outright "did you mean me?"
Carrick has to manage the delicate dressing room dynamic at a point when he needs a collective focus on trying to win enough matches to keep him in a job.
Sources who know the United boss well are adamant there is no better person to handle the turmoil, and it is at times of crisis like this that his innate calmness is a major strength.
However, after five games without a win, it is a problem Carrick could do without.
United sources say the 55-year-old is not in any danger of losing his job.

The club's recruitment department is working on potential targets for January given it is accepted the strategy of not signing left-back competition for Luke Shaw and striking support for Benjamin Sesko was flawed.

Both players have missed matches already this term, with Sesko sidelined for an indefinite period after suffering a recurrence of the shin issue that flared up in May and prevented him from playing any part in United's pre-season matches.
Unlike other major footballing countries on the continent, there is no expectation for sporting or technical directors to speak to the media.
Former United sporting director Dan Ashworth did it once during his five months at the club and was sitting alongside chief executive Omar Berrada.
Wilcox's only extensive interview since he was appointed in April 2024 has been with United's in-house media, when a couple of answers stood out.
"I am a coach at heart," said the former Blackburn Rovers and Leeds United winger, who spent several years working in coaching at Manchester City's academy.

"I am a coach inside, even though I know I have a different job now. That is a strength in my role, but it also causes me a bit of a problem because I always want to interfere in what the managers are doing."
Regarding his strategy for dealing with stress, Wilcox said: "My wife will know when I am bogged down with frustration. When I re-energise, I do it on my own. Me and the dog, walking."

Wilcox has only spoken briefly to the media after matches on a couple of occasions: after the 2-1 win at Crystal Palace last November, when he told journalists to "trust the process"; then again in Gothenburg after the pre-season encounter with Paris St-Germain when he enthused about the potential pairing of Tielemans and skipper Bruno Fernandes.

Recruitment was praised in summer 2025, when Senne Lammens was signed ahead of Emi Martinez, who was Amorim's preference, and Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo, plus Sesko, reinvigorated United's attack.

But the jury is out on the players acquired in the £155m summer outlay this year: Baleba, who missed the first six weeks of the season with injury; Santos, who has been an unused substitute in the last three Premier League games; and Tielemans, whose form has been patchy.

Sources have questioned the overall strategy, and specifically why Tielemans, who has a similar profile to England international Kobbie Mainoo, was signed, even for £35m, and if the £50m committed to Santos would have been better spent on someone who would be a first choice.
Trust is eroding among United fans over the minority ownership, agreed on Christmas Eve in 2023.
They might look at the other clubs where Ineos have an influence.
Nice are ninth in the French league and Lausanne-Sport are bottom in Switzerland. This doesn't generate a sense of a wider footballing vision that is paying dividends.

At Old Trafford, questions are being asked for the third season in a row over managers who were backed by the hierarchy in the summer. Erik ten Hag was sacked after nine Premier League games in 2024. Amorim went after 20 matches last season.

news.title: Fifa to offer extra £2.6bn for football development
news.desc: Fifa is set to propose a $3.4bn increase in the amount of money it hands out for football development across the world.
text: Fifa is set to propose a $3.4bn (£2.6bn) increase in the amount of money it hands out for football development across the world.
World football's governing body wants to release the money from its reserves in a move which would more than double the level of planned distribution funding for 2027-2030.
It says it has been able to release the extra cash because of the commercial success of this summer's World Cup.

The proposal will be made at a meeting of Fifa's council on Thursday and comes at a time when the organisation is under pressure following president Gianni Infantino's aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan.

Infantino wanted to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors but faced huge criticism for the proposal, with Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation questioning his position.
Uefa and Concacaf wrote to Infantino in September calling on Fifa to pay at least $10m (£7.5m) from its cash reserves to each of the 211 member associations.

In a letter then sent to Fifa's six continental confederations, Infantino - who will be standing for re-election for a fourth time in March 2027 - said he would support "the greatest level of additional funding that can responsibly be delivered".

Fifa will now offer extra money from its reserves in addition to the current $2.7bn (£2.05bn) budgeted to be paid to all 211 member associations, the confederations, regional associations and certain non-Fifa affiliated associations.
In total, Fifa will now be spending $6.35bn (£4.83bn) on football development for the 2027-2030 cycle, with a focus on investment and development of women's and youth football.
• $8.25m (£6.3m) for each of the 13 zonal/regional associations
• $1.1m (£836,000) for 100 member associations for travel and equipment solidarity
• One third would be allocated to women's and youth football development
• One third would be allocated to infrastructure (of which there shall be equal access to women's and youth football)
The plan, including the eligibility, application, approval, disbursement, control and audit requirements, will be finalised by the Fifa council at its next meeting in December 2026.
It will all be subject to approval by the 77th Fifa congress in March 2027.

BBC Sport understands there is a proposal on the table at the council to change the disciplinary code and prevent a repeat of the Folarin Balogun situation, an unprecedented scenario which meant the US striker did not miss a game after being sent off in the World Cup.
If approved, it will be expressly noted in the regulations that an automatic one-match ban for a red card cannot be suspended.
Questions have been raised over the process which led to Balogun having his ban suspended.
US President Donald Trump said he called Infantino to get the ban rescinded, which raised serious concerns over political interference.
A proposal has been put forward to add to Article 27 of the regulations a list of instances whereby a ban cannot be suspended.
Infantino broke trust 'through deception' - confederation presidents

news.title: Cokayne back as England face Canada threat in Toronto
news.desc: England welcome back the experience of Amy Cokayne at hooker as their 41-match unbeaten run comes under serious threat away to Canada.
text: England welcome back the experienced Amy Cokayne at hooker as their 41-match unbeaten run goes on the line against Rugby World Cup runners-up Canada in Toronto on Friday.
Cokayne has not played Test rugby since scoring the Red Roses' final try in a Grand Slam-sealing win over France in Bordeaux in May.
Saracens' Bryony Field, who has three caps to Cokayne's 94, drops to the bench after deputising impressively in the first half of the WXV Global Series last month.
During that part of the campaign, Canada ended England's near four-year winning streak with a nail-biting 26-26 draw at Sandy Park in Exeter.
Coach Kevin Rouet has targeted victory over the Red Roses as the main aim for Canada in 2026, with his team playing on home soil for the first time in more than 14 months.
Canada also play England in Ottawa on Friday, 23 October, with the two matches branded as the hosts' Rugby Rematch Tour.

The attendance for the Toronto match is expected to exceed 14,000, comfortably beating the previous record for a standalone women's rugby match in North America which was set when 11,453 watched Canada beat the United States in the most recent home match.
Elsewhere in England's line-up, prop Hannah Botterman features after coming on as a replacement in the dramatic win over New Zealand last time out.

With Marlie Packer staying in England as her partner and Red Roses team-mate Rosie Galligan is due to give birth, Abi Burton takes a spot in the back row, while Tatyana Heard's direct running is preferred to Helena Rowland's playmaking ability at inside centre.
Sadia Kabeya, who missed the win over the Black Ferns with a leg injury, is on the bench, alongside Bristol Bears' 20-year-old Demelza Short, who covers second row.
"The first Test in Exeter gave us a valuable opportunity to test our game under pressure and identify where we can improve," England head coach John Mitchell said.
"Playing in Toronto presents a different environment and challenge, and we're excited by the opportunity to express our game, improve our performance and continue to grow as the Red Roses."
England's last loss came in the Rugby World Cup final against New Zealand in November 2022.
England: Kildunne; Breach, Jones, Heard, Moloney-MacDonald; Harrison, L Packer; Botterman, Cokayne, Bern, Talling, Ives Campion, Burton, Matthews, Feaunati.
Replacements: Field, Carson, Muir, Short, Kabeya, Hunt, Rowland, Sing.
