news.title: Millwall's Neil criticised over racial abuse stoppage comments
news.desc: Anti-racism campaign group Kick It Out calls on managers to "set the tone" after Millwall boss Alex Neil criticises halting a game following an accusation of abuse.
text: Anti-racism campaign group Kick It Out has called on football managers to "set the tone" after Millwall boss Alex Neil criticised the decision to halt their game against Swansea City following an accusation of racist abuse.

Tuesday's Championship match was brought to a standstill for seven minutes, midway through the second half, after reports of discriminatory chants directed at Swansea substitute Ji-sung Eom, which the Metropolitan Police is investigating.
After the game, Neil told BBC Radio London: "It needs to get dealt with. [But] stopping the game doesn't deal with anything. All it does is kill the momentum."

A statement from Kick It Out said: "Player welfare should always take precedence over the momentum or flow of a match, and it's essential that managers and all leaders recognise this and set the tone with their language so that everyone can stand up to discrimination."

When he was alerted to the accusations, referee Edward Duckworth had lengthy discussions with both sets of coaches and paused the match while he waited to pass a message on to Millwall's safety officer.
Following the stoppage, an announcement was made over the speakers at The Den confirming there had been alleged chants of racism and that police were working to identify any offenders using CCTV.
"I understand, obviously, there's been an incident," Neil said. "That's not something I'm going to get involved in - that'll be for the authorities to deal with.
"But the fact that it stops the game, I just don't see the point.
"The referee was wanting to speak to whoever the safety officer is, and then when he spoke to him, it [the game] restarted.
"That's partly my frustration. I want to get the game restarted, I want to get the game played.
"I understand there's other things that are going on, but you're not dealing with it down there, are you? It's going to get dealt with after the event anyway."
After the match restarted, Millwall went on to concede a 90th-minute goal to lose 1-0.
"If we score, I probably don't feel this way, let's be honest," Neil added.
Kick It Out, which has campaigned for more than 30 years to eradicate racism from football, said it was disappointed to hear reports of racist abuse towards Eom.

"Both clubs have condemned the incident, and it's positive that Millwall and match officials followed the right protocols so that action can be taken to identify any individual responsible," the organisation said.
"In that moment, protocols are in place to help match and security officials respond appropriately.
"That ensures that players are protected and key details are captured so that accountability can follow, regardless of how long it takes."
Millwall stated they were "aware of an alleged, individual incident of discriminatory abuse towards a Swansea City player during the second half" of the game.
"The club operates a zero-tolerance policy towards any form of discriminatory abuse," a club statement said after the game.
"Any individual found to have engaged in such behaviour will face the strongest possible action."
Swansea City head coach Vitor Matos praised the referee and Millwall's club staff for their responses to the incident.
"The referee followed the protocol for these sort of situations, they did the right thing," he said.
"Millwall did the right thing by announcing there is no place for this sort of thing. I'm happy with how it was handled, but really sad that it happened."

news.title: Aston Villa run riot in record-breaking win over Fenerbahce as Mason Greenwood taunted on UK return
news.desc: Aston Villa hit Fenerbahce for six on a memorable night at Villa Park
text: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in
Aston Villa hit Fenerbahce for six on a memorable night at Villa Park
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Mason Greenwood suffered a miserable return to English football as his Fenerbahce team were swept aside 6-0 by a rampant Aston Villa side in the Champions League.

The 25-year-old was playing his first match in this country since his suspension by Manchester United in January 2022, facing taunts from home fans who thoroughly enjoyed an electric Villa Park display.
Johan Manzambi marked his 21st birthday with a goal before Nicolas Jackson scored a double to give Villa a 3-0 lead at half-time.
A second-half brace from Ross Barkley and a late finish by Tammy Abraham completed the rout over the Turkish side, delighting the Prince of Wales, who gave his royal seal of approval from the stands.

It was Villa’s largest ever European victory and provided their first home win of the season. The result leaves them strongly positioned in the early Champions League standings with two victories from two, ahead of an inviting home game against Viking next week.
Villa supporters ensured Greenwood was given a hostile reception on his return to playing in England after four-and-a-half years.
The winger’s last appearance for United came in January 2022, eight days before he was charged with attempted rape, controlling and coercive behaviour and assault occasioning actual bodily harm.
He denied the charges, and the CPS discontinued the case in February 2023.
The Villa crowd targeted him with persistent boos and derogatory chants during the opening period.
The home support soon turned their attention to celebrating as Villa’s energetic start yielded a 12th-minute opener.
John McGinn’s corner landed for birthday boy Manzambi, whose shot took a deflection off Milan Skriniar and went in.
Fenerbahce offered a bright response with chances to equalise, but Vedat Muriqi was twice thwarted by Zion Suzuki, who also dealt with a weak strike by Greenwood.
Villa doubled their advantage in the 31st minute when Jackson got off the mark.
Boubacar Kamara dispossessed the opposition high up the pitch and found the former Chelsea striker, who drilled a low shot into the bottom corner from 18 yards.
The Turkish side remained a constant threat and ought to have scored soon after, but Oguz Aydin crashed his shot against the crossbar after breaking behind the Villa defence.
Instead, Villa were left celebrating once more as they made it 3-0 in the 39th minute.
McGinn reclaimed possession and Barkley set up Jackson, who placed his finish into a similar spot to his first goal.
Villa had to wait until the 68th minute to score a fourth, though Jackson – who was on a hat-trick – did not take the penalty after Manzambi was fouled by Ismail Yuksek.
Instead, Barkley converted from the spot and four minutes later he scored again as a deflected strike from the edge of the area wrong-footed former Manchester City goalkeeper Ederson.
Abraham completed an emphatic victory in the 90th minute, turning the ball in from close range after fine work by winger Alysson.

news.title: Man City v PSG LIVE: Wild six-goal thriller in Champions League enthralls returning Pep Guardiola
news.desc: Manchester City 2-4 Paris Saint-Germain: PSG were made to hang on after their first-half masterclass as Erling Haaland scored twice and had many chances to complete his hat-trick
text: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in
Manchester City 2-4 Paris Saint-Germain: PSG were made to hang on after their first-half masterclass as Erling Haaland scored twice and had many chances to complete his hat-trick
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Paris Saint-Germain produced a statement first-half display before Manchester City threatened a remarkable comeback in a thrilling second-half performance as the Champions League holders ran out 4-2 winners at the Etihad.

City were initially blown away in front of the returning former City boss Pep Guardiola as Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha struck for the visitors and Achraf Hakimi hit the post in a rampant 17-minute spell, with PSG becoming the first team to score three first-half goals against City away from home since Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool in November 2015.

Enzo Maresca made a triple change at the break and it sparked an improved showing from City, who pulled one back when Erling Haaland headed in and had several chances to score another. City goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma was then unable to keep out a shot from Maghnes Akliouche as PSG scored a fourth, but Haaland pulled another back for City shortly after he had hit the bar.

Haaland was denied a hat-trick as PSG goalkeeper Matveii Safonov produced a point-blank save and there was still time for former City forward Ferran Torres to roll a tame penalty straight at Donnarumma after Spain’s World Cup winner had been handed the chance to make it five for the European champions.

City were playing their first match at home since they were found guilty of almost all of the club’s breaches of the Premier League financial rules. With City appealing the decision and continuing to maintain their innocence, Maresca’s side were supported by former manager Guardiola, who returned to the Etihad for the first time since his departure in May and looked typically on edge in the stands as he enjoyed a six-goal thriller.
Elsewhere on a very busy night of Champions League action, here’s how it all finished...

City had 27 shots, PSG 15, with nine and 10 on target respectively. Plus 52 and 17 touches in the opposition box respectively. Big night for all-out attacking football. The less said about the defending, the better...
In the midst of all that, Haaland became City’s all-time record goalscorer in the Champions League.
Luis Enrique and Enzo Maresca share a warm hug. Donnarumma has a nice chat with his former teammates, no bad blood there.
‘90: O’Reilly, who has been preparing to come on for the last eight minutes or so, comes on for Fernandez.
‘89: Nunes does bring him down, sliding in, but he can’t believe it, and you’ve certainly seen more concrete penalties not given. But it stands.
Ex-City man Ferran Torres is resoundingly booed as he steps up to take it... it’s a poor attempt and Donnarumma saves it!!
‘88: PSG counter. Matheus Nunes goes sliding in on Nuno Mendes, who goes down in the box. The referee points to the spot!
The City players swarm around the referee. VAR is looking at it...
‘86: More pin-ball in the box, Haaland tees up Semenyo, who loses it under pressure from two defenders, and eventually leans back too far and slams it over the bar.

news.title: How Bradley Barcola scored his Liverpool hat-trick, but were defensive lapses a concern?
news.desc: LASK 3-6 Liverpool: Andoni Iraola’s side enjoyed a big Champions League win as Lewis Koumas also got on the scoresheet in Austria
text: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in
LASK 3-6 Liverpool: Andoni Iraola’s side enjoyed a big Champions League win as Lewis Koumas also got on the scoresheet in Austria
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Bradley Barcola got off the mark for Liverpool in style with a Champions League hat-trick in a 6-3 win against LASK in Austria.
The France international winger did not score in his first five appearances for the Reds after arriving from Paris Saint-Germain in deal that could rise to £123m.
But the 24-year-old bagged his first senior hat-trick of his career as Liverpool ran riot against the Austrian champions.
Defender Ronald Araujo also scored his first Liverpool goal with the first of the night, while Jeremie Frimpong and Lewis Koumas were also on target for Andoni Iraola’s side.
Welsh forward Koumas, who started in place of the injured Alexander Isak, scored his first Liverpool goal in two-and-a-half years after the 21-year-old had two goals ruled out earlier.
While Liverpool’s forward line threatened all night, there was sloppiness at the back in the closing stages and Iraola will be disappointed to have conceded three for the second game in a row.
But a second consecutive win in the Champions League, following the opening victory over Atletico Madrid, got Iraola’s side back on track following Sunday’s 3-0 defeat to Manchester City.
Ironically, the standout winger on the night was arguably Rio Ngumoha, with the 18-year-old tormenting LASK throughout with his direct dribbling and trickery out wide.
But it was Barcola who produced the clinical touches in the area, adding to his electric bursts of speed and movement behind the LASK backline.
Ngumoha was the spark for Barcola’s first Liverpool goal, working his way into the box before a clever flick from Koumas allowed Barcola to sweep a first-time finish into the far corner.
Barcola’s second was created by Florian Wirtz, who responded to the criticism of his performance against City with a piercing through ball between LASK defenders and into Barcola’s feet.
After his earlier strike, two quick touches from the former PSG winger displayed his confidence and eye for goal, with a low left-footed finish slotted into the bottom corner.
Barcola’s third to complete the hat-trick was the simplest of the three, owing to being in the right place at the right time after Ngumoha had slipped in Frimpong to square across goal.
“I think he played so well today and not just the goals,” Iraola said of Barcola’s performance. “He had more chances to score and he was always a threat attacking the spaces in behind.
“In training sometimes you feel when a player is in the zone, and fortunately tonight for us he has shown the level that he has.”
Koumas was rewarded for another committed performance leading the line and the academy product showed how much a Champions League goal meant for the Reds with his celebration.
“He has to enjoy it because he deserves it,” Iraola said. “I think he scored two disallowed goals which is unlucky for him but he kept pressing, making the runs in behind and doing his job.
“I think it’s fair that he score his goal and can have his moment of celebration with the supporters.”
In all, it added up to a pleasing attacking performance for Iraola, with Ngumoha and Koumas again impressing in the absence of Isak and Cody Gakpo and Barcola and Wirtz making impacts too.
“I’m very happy with the performance,” Iraola added. “Today I think we were very aggressive with the ball. Sometimes you talk aggressiveness without the ball but I’m talking about with the ball.
“I think we took good positions, we moved the ball well, attacked the spaces well.”
Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk was given a rare evening off, with left-back Kostas Tsimikas wearing the armband in his absence and Araujo and Jeremy Jacquet starting at centre-back.
Jacquet continued his excellent start to life at Liverpool with another impressing while Araujo’s first goal, rising from a corner to head in the delivery from Tsimikas, was a bonus as well.
Where it went wrong defensively for Liverpool, having largely dominated LASK from the outset, was when Iraola made changes to the backline while the Reds were leading 4-0.
It is unusual to see a centre-back pair swapped mid-game but Van Dijk and Joe Gomez were brought on for Jacquet and Araujo in a double-change on the hour.
Liverpool were immediately caught cold as Robert Ljubicic pulled one back. Then, after Barcola and Koumas had stretched Liverpool’s lead to 6-1, Florian Flecker struck twice for the hosts.
Both goals looked preventable, sure, and Alisson conceded three times from four shots on target.
But given the game had been won and Liverpool were already looking towards Saturday’s trip to Brentford in the Premier League, they won’t be too much of a concern.
“It’s probably the reason why the manager shouldn’t change both centre-backs!” Iraola said.
“But we were already winning 4-0 and you have to think about the next game and saving the legs of the players. We didn’t defend properly at the end of the game."

news.title: ‘An exhibition’: Steven Gerrard salutes PSG after stunning first half against Man City
news.desc: Doue, Dembele and Vitinha struck for the back-to-back Champions League winners, in the first time City had conceded three first-half goals at home since 2015
text: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in
Doue, Dembele and Vitinha struck for the back-to-back Champions League winners, in the first time City had conceded three first-half goals at home since 2015
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Steven Gerrard hailed “a 31-minute exhibition” from Paris Saint-Germain as the best football he had seen in years after the Champions League holders scored three first-half goals against Manchester City.
Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha struck for the visitors and Achraf Hakimi hit the post in a rampant 17-minute spell while former City manager Pep Guardiola watched on at the Etihad.

Guardiola was making his first appearance at the Etihad since leaving the club in May, in what was City’s first home appearance since the were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules.

But PSG became the first team to score three first-half goals against Manchester City away from home since Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool in November 2015 as Luis Enrique’s back-to-back champions produced a statement performance.

And former Liverpool captain Gerrard was stunned to see a City side who have won all six of their Premier League games this season and were 3-0 winners at Anfield on Sunday be so comprehensively outplayed.

“It’s been a 31-minute exhibition, it’s been so one-sided,” Gerrard said on TNT Sports. “Outstanding. I think Enzo Maresca has to speak to his staff and change something. I think they’re a man down in the centre of the pitch with [Rayan] Cherki.”

Former England international Owen Hargreaves called PSG’s football “ridiculous” and said: “The quality of the touches and finishing [from PSG] is exquisite. That is as good as I’ve seen live maybe ever. Technically this is best of what the Premier League has to offer and they’ve put on a masterclass.”

news.title: Arsenal cutting jobs just days after Mikel Arteta’s £80m deal is simply indefensible
news.desc: The Premier League champions have told staff of plans to cut at least 60 jobs, writes Miguel Delaney , which completely goes against the club’s traditional values of ‘doing things the right way’
text: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in
The Premier League champions have told staff of plans to cut at least 60 jobs, writes Miguel Delaney, which completely goes against the club’s traditional values of ‘doing things the right way’
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
The contrasts couldn’t be worse, and run right through Arsenal. Above all, though, there are the headline numbers.

A mere five days after Mikel Arteta signed one of the most lucrative managerial contracts in football, a £20m per year deal amid all manner of pageantry, the club staged a call to announce plans to cut 60 jobs - although there is the potential for this to come down.
People on everyday wages are now fearing for their jobs and mortgages, as the show just goes on.

Many staff members had feared this for some time, especially since the expensive consultancy firm Boston Consultancy Group [BCG] had been brought to examine the business earlier this year, but that seemed to jar with how – in the words of multiple sources – the football side has been “more and more indulged”.

The men’s and women’s performance departments, which represent well over half of the club's outgoings, isn’t to be touched in this round of redundancies. The manager has total control there, anyway, and did admittedly make considerable changes in the summer.
Arsenal had even planned for a blockbuster move for Real Madrid forward Vinicius Jr in the summer, and one of the lines at the time was that the wages could be made up on image rights alone.
Now, the image of the club is sullied, as employees under threat of losing wages that would barely pay for two days of some Arsenal stars.
“You’re concentrating on the 10 per cent of the club, where most of the people are on everyday wages,” as one insider says.
This is always one of the most galling things when any major club plans such cuts, as was the case with Arsenal themselves back in 2020.
Or, as one source put it, you’d spend years trying to make up the money that went out on contracts for Fabio Vieira, Reiss Neilson and so many others.
“Players were on £100,000 a week to be crash test dummies in training”, a source said.
That might be football, sure, but the point is it doesn’t need to impinge on staff lives. That’s where it’s, once again, indefensible.
It’s even worse when the last accounts showed a club-record revenue of £691m. Arsenal are expected to reach £800m next.

The rationale behind this is said to be “cost efficiency” rather than “cost cutting” and to take the club to a next stage. And while 60 is the current number, that could come down, while it is possible that a lot of the roles could be redeployed.
As one insider says, however, “this wasn’t necessary and cuts more muscle than fat, potentially bringing more cost than benefit”. And it is still people losing jobs.
So much for success on the pitch translating into health off it, as has previously been seen at comparable models like Liverpool.
The celebratory mood from May’s long-awaited title is so quickly undercut by gloom about this.
That aspect is something that shouldn’t be overlooked in such stories, even if it should be secondary to concerns over people’s livelihoods.
Arteta talks about club “culture” probably more than any manager, and he has worked hard to build up that identity again, but these kinds of decisions directly corrode that.

Arsenal only have to ask counterparts at Manchester United. Those close to Sir Jim Ratcliffe say there was eventually some regret at the cuts they made, because it didn’t really achieve anything other than dismal headlines and a worse mood.
It affected the sense of unity that is actually crucial to sport, as well as the sense of community that these social institutions are supposed to stand for.
Most of them, under modern ownerships, often behave rather differently.
It is the crucial intangible that these kinds of hierarchies miss when striving for “efficiency”, as the BCG consultancy was intended to achieve.

And this is where the entire story is so integral to wider themes, from the Independent Football Regulator publishing a “State of the Game” review that is specifically intended to protect clubs’ community roles, to a debate about ownership that has been sharpened by the Manchester City crisis.
Much of this comes down to classic American corporatism, the ownership type that represents the other major force imposing itself on football in parallel to Gulf state wealth.
You can repeat all of the known lines about such leaderships only ever being interested in growth, when that is not what a football club exists for.

A football club – even the biggest in the world – only exist to play football for the local community they represent. They don’t actually need to do anything more to be sustainable, which a club with an immense global fanbase can obviously be. And that in a game awash with money due to that unique global popularity.

The business element is only something that has been bolted on over the past 30 years, as old rules on directors – that Friar lived through – were bypassed by stock market flotation and the rise of the Premier League.
Numerous insiders still say this is all even more acute with Kroenke Sports and Entertainment.
Stan Kroenke, the patriarch whose main background is real estate, has always been obsessed with margins.
Those on the American side of their sports empire state this has often been centred on numbers, and especially staff.
Moves like this are an inevitable consequence, and feel all the worse when they so jar with Arsenal’s self image of “doing things the right way”.
Other sources put it in the context of considerable change at executive level over the past year, which has created new pressures.
Kroenke likes low margins, and here are the margins being made lower, even if they are infinitesimal.
CEO Richard Garlick has been a corporate face of late, doing a series of media appearances and conferences to talk about how the club was transformed over the past half-decade.
Only last week, at Leaders at Stamford Bridge, he was talking about how this is only a beginning and the club now needed to show "confidence".
Well, what's this? This round of redundancies is something the old traditional Arsenal would not have considered.

news.title: Vinicius Jr to miss El Clasico against Barcelona after receiving four-game ban
news.desc: The Real Madrid winger will miss the games against Sevilla, Barcelona, Racing Santander ⁠and Valencia after his red card on Saturday
text: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in
The Real Madrid winger will miss the games against Sevilla, Barcelona, Racing Santander ⁠and Valencia after his red card on Saturday
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Vinicius Jr will miss Real Madrid’s first Clasico of the season against Barcelona after the Spanish Football Federation’s disciplinary committee handed the Brazil forward a four-match suspension on Wednesday.
The attacker was sent off for pulling the hair of Nathan Saliba after coming off the bench during Saturday's 1-0 win over Villarreal.

The committee handed down a two-match ban for the red card and added a further two games for his protests to the referee, according to the disciplinary report from the eighth round of LaLiga fixtures.

The suspension rules Vinicius out of league matches against Sevilla, Barcelona, Racing Santander and Valencia, leaving coach Jose Mourinho without one of his most heavily used forwards for the trip to Camp Nou.
Vinicius has started all but one of Real’s matches this season.
The winger was celebrating his second goal of the match against Villarreal when referee Isidro Diaz de Mera was summoned by the video assistant to examine the build-up to the strike.
The goal was ultimately disallowed after review showed Vinicius Jr pulling the hair of Saliba as they sprinted down the field.
A straight red card was then shown to Vinicius Jr, forcing Madrid to play with 10 men from the 73rd minute onwards.
The dismissal led to angry confrontations on the pitch as the forward shouted at Diaz de Mera while teammates attempted to restrain him.
Manager Jose Mourinho had initially joined the goal celebrations, but the decision left him incensed.
He subsequently missed the mandatory post-match press conference, reportedly out of concern that making comments about the refereeing would trigger a suspension.
The manager had already been shown a yellow card earlier in the fixture and was repeatedly restrained by backroom staff after prior decisions were made against his team.
Following the incident, he used social media to apologise to his teammates and Real Madrid fans.
The Clasico takes place on 25 October, with Real travelling to .eague leaders Barcelona

news.title: Fifa poised for rule change to avoid Folarin Balogun scandal repeat
news.desc: Folarin Balogun’s World Cup ban was suspended after Donald Trump revealed he called Gianni Infantino over the red card
text: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in
Folarin Balogun’s World Cup ban was suspended after Donald Trump revealed he called Gianni Infantino over the red card
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Fifa is preparing to alter its regulations to prevent any repeat of the controversy surrounding Folarin Balogun.

A dispute over political interference erupted after Fifa’s disciplinary committee opted to suspend an automatic one-match ban handed to the United States forward during the World Cup. The intervention came after US president Donald Trump publicly disclosed that he had personally phoned Fifa counterpart Gianni Infantino to request a review of the decision.
A proposal to explicitly prohibit the suspension of automatic one-game bans in the future is expected to be introduced at Thursday’s Fifa Council meeting in Zurich.

However, the regulatory change alone is unlikely to satisfy critics seeking a full explanation of how Balogun’s suspension was set aside. Among those seeking answers is Football Association chair and Fifa vice-president Debbie Hewitt, who wrote to Infantino last month requesting the disclosure of all documents related to the case.
Infantino has consistently maintained that the disciplinary panel reached its decision independently of his office.

Hewitt and fellow Council members are also expected to press Infantino for further details regarding the abandoned Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal. The initiative aimed to bring private investment into a commercial arm that would oversee the financial rights of the World Cup and other major tournaments.

The Swiss official faced calls to step down over the summer from the presidents of three continental confederations, including Uefa, after details of the FFE plan - developed without consulting the Fifa Council - were disclosed in media reports.

While Infantino appeared under severe pressure initially, he remains intent on standing for a fourth term as president at next year’s Fifa Congress and holds a strong position. Last week, he secured unanimous backing from the Confederation of African Football (CAF), alongside robust support across South America, Oceania, and Asia.

The president of the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa, who urged Infantino to resign in August, appeared to soften his stance last month in a letter advocating for an internal working group to explore governance reforms.
Uefa has committed to putting forward a credible opposition candidate before the 18 November deadline, but Infantino presents a formidable challenge for any contender.
The Fifa Peace Prize is also listed for discussion on Thursday following a request from a Council member.
Reports indicate the Council is seeking clarity on the process for this year's award, which was presented to President Trump for the first time last December.
Infantino may also face questioning regarding Fifa’s lease for office space in New York's Trump Tower, where the governing body reportedly agreed to pay $4 million (just over £3m) over seven years.
Additionally, reports surfaced this week that Infantino received a £1.3m payment in 2024 from an American Fifa World Cup subsidiary company that was omitted from Fifa’s annual financial report.

The Council is also set to consider a proposal from Fifa administrators to distribute $6.35 billion (£4.8bn) to member nations and continental confederations over the next three years, including $25 million (£19m) to each of Fifa’s 211 member countries.
That allocation would more than double the amount originally scheduled for distribution in the 2027 to 2030 cycle.

The plan follows a letter sent to Infantino on 18 September by the presidents of Uefa and Concacaf, urging that every national association receive an additional $10 million (£7.6m) through a single release from Fifa’s cash reserves, estimated at $6 billion (£4.5bn).

Aleksander Ceferin and Victor Montagliani stated that releasing the funds would demonstrate that member bodies "should not have to choose between development and good governance; between investment and integrity; or between financial support and the ability to consider proposals on their merits".
The remarks were seen as a direct reference to FFE, as Fifa had previously pledged increased development funding to federations if the project was approved.
Fifa has been approached for comment on the proposed financial increase.
The Council is also expected to confirm host nations for several competitions, including the inaugural Women’s Club World Cup in 2028, with the US regarded as the front-runner to stage the event.

news.title: Liverpool led by surprise new captain amid Virgil van Dijk absence and Alisson ruling
news.desc: Goalkeeper Alisson Becker is technically Liverpool’s vice-captain, but he will not wear the armband when the Reds face LASK in the Champions League
text: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in
Goalkeeper Alisson Becker is technically Liverpool’s vice-captain, but he will not wear the armband when the Reds face LASK in the Champions League
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Kostas Tsimikas will captain Liverpool for the first time as the Reds play Austrian side LASK in the Champions League on Tuesday.
The Greek left-back, who scored the winning penalty in the 2022 FA Cup final but spent last season out on loan with Roma, wears the armband with Virgil van Dijk on the bench.
Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola confirmed before the season that he had named Alisson Becker his vice-captain following the departures of Mohamed Salah and Andy Robertson.
But Iraola explained that the goalkeeper would never actually wear the armband on the pitch due to rules that mean only the captains can talk to the referee on the pitch.

“I explained to Alisson especially that it’s not going to be possible that he wears the armband because with the new rule I think there is a big limitation if a keeper wears the armband,” Iraola said in August.
“Because if something happens in the opposition box the referee has to explain to the captains what’s happening, all the decisions.
“I had one season with [goalkeeper] Neto [as captain] in Bournemouth and then you have to start every game to say a different player that can act as a captain, and this is not viable.

“But I wanted him to feel like we value him. I’ve had enough time and we will have more time to know each other, but I had to explain also the decision about the armband to Ali because he is a keeper and, unfortunately, they are putting the rules in a way that there is a lot of disadvantages to having a keeper as a captain.”
The 30-year-old Tsimikas joined Liverpool in 2020 and is the longest-serving outfield player starting for the Reds in Austria.
Iraola confirmed before the start of the season that Dominik Szoboszlai and Joe Gomez were also among his vice-captains, but Gomez is on the bench while Szoboszlai remains injured.
Tsimikas wore the armband in pre-season, taking the captaincy from Gomez after the defender was forced off with an injury in the game against Sunderland.
Liverpool XI: Alisson, Frimpong, Jacquet, Araujo, Tsimikas; Gravenberch, Nyoni; Ngumoha, Wirtz, Barcola; Koumas
Subs: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Gomez, Van Dijk, Kerkez, Mac Allister, Munoz, Chambers, McConnell, Danns, Sonni-Lambie, Lucky.

Arbeloa made the comments about match officials following Fulham’s 1-1 draw with Manchester United last month

Fulham manager Alvaro Arbeloa has received a £25,000 FA fine and a warning on Wednesday for post-match comments questioning the integrity of the referee following last month’s Premier League match against Manchester United.
Arbeloa accepted a charge that he had "acted in an improper manner" through remarks made after the 1-1 draw between the sides at Craven Cottage on 20 September.
"I think all fouls for them," the Spaniard stated following the match, in reference to United, who had lost to Manchester City the previous weekend due to a contentious goal.
"Every decision was for them," Arbeloa added, "and I knew, I knew after the game against Man City that they don’t let Manchester United lose here."

Written reasons published on Wednesday showed the independent commission investigating the incident "felt that those words suggested, not only that there was bias on the part of the match officials throughout the game on repeated occasions, but also that there may even have been an element of pre-meditation by them and/or others to try to make up for an error in a different match."
Arbeloa is currently in his first season at Fulham having left Real Madrid over the summer.

Fulham are currently bottom of the table after taking just two points from their opening six games. One of those draws came against United, while they also earned a point away at Liverpool. They have been beaten by Chelsea, Sunderland, Crystal Palace and Ipswich Town.

Arbeloa’s side are due to return to action when they host newly-promoted Hull City on Saturday at Craven Cottage. They will then face another promoted club, Coventry City, seven days later before playing Crystal Palace in the Carabao Cup for a spot in the quarter-finals of the competition.
Fulham’s final match in October will be a trip to Aston Villa.

Meanwhile, Manchester United have failed to bounce back after last month’s draw at Fulham. Since returning from the international break, Michael Carrick’s side have been held to a 1-1 draw by 10-man Tottenham, and they were then beaten 2-0 by Atletico Madrid in the Champions League on Tuesday.

news.title: Lisandro Martinez’s extraordinary rant told the truth about Man United’s inept hierarchy
news.desc: Comment: Martinez pointed the finger at the club’s board after Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid – and Chris Wilson explains why the defender was right to be so critical
text: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in
Comment: Martinez pointed the finger at the club’s board after Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid – and Chris Wilson explains why the defender was right to be so critical
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
After a summer that promised so much, Manchester United have arrived in an autumn of discontent. Just as it looked like they might be turning a corner, they’re back to square one.

Tuesday’s Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid may well put Michael Carrick on the brink of losing his job. Several United players – notably captain Bruno Fernandes – looked totally dejected at full-time – and that was before Lisandro Martinez decided to launch an astonishing attack on the club’s ownership.

The result leaves United with just two wins from their opening nine games of the season, with those coming against newly promoted Ipswich and Champions League debutants Sabah. It is a far cry from the team that won 12 of their last 17 Premier League games on their way to finishing third last term.

“Sometimes it’s a reflection of the mirror of how is our club at the moment, you know?” Martinez said to Prime Video in Madrid. “We did a fantastic season last season and now we expect more from the top. I expect more, 100 per cent. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox].”

It was a surprising tirade from the Argentine, though one most United fans will agree with. And while it signals real discontent among the players, Carrick was quick to emphasise how together the squad is in terms of matters on the pitch. The players clearly back their manager too, with Martinez saying that United “can't keep changing, changing, changing the manager”.

While Carrick’s tactics and his role in United’s downturn in form will rightly face scrutiny, it’s clear that this is not an issue of a player revolt against the manager, but rather disillusionment over the actions of those at the top of the club.

This will hurt Ineos and the likes of Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell, mostly because Martinez is undeniably correct. United spent a portion of the summer pursuing Elliot Anderson, only to see him move to rivals Manchester City, while they instead signed Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba for a combined total of around £150m for a different type of midfield rebuild.

A few weeks later, only Baleba looks up to the required standard. Spending £50m on Santos – a player who could not get regular starts for Chelsea – when other parts of the squad needed investment now looks staggeringly inept – especially if Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko are injured.

United did not invest in a forward despite plenty of evidence that Joshua Zirkzee is not good enough for their ambitions, and they failed in their pursuit of Lewis Hall, leaving themselves with only one recognised left-back in the squad.

The rest of the defence was an afterthought, with reports emerging that the hierarchy are planning a defensive rebuild next summer. It would appear a naive approach. You can’t expect every signing to work out, but this strategy simply suggests that some key people do not know how to run a football club.

That is the core complaint from Martinez, with others – notably Fernandes – also seemingly frustrated at the start of this season. You suspect Carrick and certain players were given assurances over investment into the squad, and yet United spent just £163m over the summer, which is less than all of their top six rivals, as well as newly-promoted clubs Hull and Ipswich.

To make matters worse, the atmosphere has soured off the pitch too, with the recent season ticketing fiasco causing a further rift between the hierarchy and fans, who feel that they’ve been treated unfairly. Bans are now extending to members. While some touts will be scuppered in this new drive, innocent fans are also getting caught out with limited time to appeal and a lack of clarity regarding what exactly has led to the accusations.

That a job advert for a “Supporter Escalations Executive” – to “support the Club's mission to tackle ticket touting” – was not filled before a huge number of investigations and bans highlights the confused, haphazard nature of work that has now characterised the club for at least the last 13 years, if not more.

Add to this the farce surrounding the hiring and firing of Dan Ashworth, as well as the cutting of 322 jobs, and Ineos are miles away from the best-in-class image they have tried to present to the outside world. It would be difficult to get away with this level of ineptitude in most other jobs.

There are mitigating factors, most notably the $1.1bn of debt lumped on the club by the Glazer family, but Ineos have not enamoured themselves with the fans, adding to the mess created by the Glazers over the last two decades or so. They are now in charge of much of the footballing side and they simply haven’t delivered – now it’s clear that the players are disillusioned too.
While Wayne Rooney was probably right in saying that Martinez’s interview “is not going to help the situation”, it might be a case where things have to get worse before they get better.

There needs to be a reckoning at United, and while the Glazers should undeniably be at the top of the list when that time comes, a number of figures associated with the minority ownership also have uncomfortable questions to answer.

news.title: Why this Champions League campaign feels very different for Manchester City
news.desc: City streak of dining at European football’s top table may be coming to an abrupt end, adding an extra layer to tonight’s clash with PSG
text: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in
City streak of dining at European football’s top table may be coming to an abrupt end, adding an extra layer to tonight’s clash with PSG
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Enzo Maresca has an idea of how, to borrow a phrase adapted from an Inspiral Carpets song, this is how it feels to be City. It has changed in the last three weeks, with a guilty verdict returned in the case of 114 Premier League charges, with an official judgment that they benefited from more than £900m in disguised, and thus illegitimate, funding, with the word “sham” attached to their contracts and, for some, their achievements.

Maresca has talked about how he and his players have had to block out the “noise”, as he terms it. They did it very effectively at Anfield on Sunday, shrugging off chants about cheating to beat Liverpool 3-0.
He accepts it is harder for the Manchester City faithful to ignore it, and not merely because the subject matter goes beyond the usual back-and-forth between followers of competing clubs.

“It probably has been more tough for our fans than for the players or for me because it's probably more complicated,” said the Italian. “Because if I am an Arsenal fan or a [Manchester] United fan and you are a City fan, I can tell you, ‘Hey, my friend, you cheat,’ or this kind of thing.”
And if that creates an image of Maresca not as a manager, but as a rival supporter, calling City cheats, his captain endured a similar soundtrack for 90 minutes on Sunday and sounded unruffled.

“I feel like when you build yourself as a player, you build yourself against any kind of noise. So be it the word you just described, or any other kind,” said Ruben Dias. “Personally, and I really feel like I speak for the whole group, we're very calm.”

How does it feel to be City, though? Top of the Premier League with a 100 percent record, having won the two away games that tend to mean most to their supporters – United and then Liverpool – and with Maresca looking a worthy successor to Pep Guardiola, they face the champions of Europe on Wednesday. Paris Saint-Germain could provided a barometer of the progress of this new-look City side.

Dias was asked if Luis Enrique’s team will win a third consecutive Champions League. “Hopefully they cannot,” he replied, speaking to his own ambitions. Yet this is more than a duel of the nouveaux riches, the last two first-time winners of the competition. They have been bracketed together for other reasons: Middle Eastern ownership from oil-rich states, heavy spending, questions if it fell within the parameters of the rules. It was not City who spent a world record €222m on Neymar.

While PSG seek to cement an era of dominance, City’s spell as Champions League ever-presents could be nearing an end: not because of their Premier League form but because of the possible sanctions for their rule-breaking; deduct enough Premier League points or expel them and their only route back into the Champions League is to win it.

“If this is the last Champions League for a while, I don't know,” said Maresca. The annual trips to the Bernabeu may be no more. PSG, beaten by City in the quarter-finals in 2016 and the semi-finals in 2021, might not be on the fixture list again for quite some time. Perhaps, after City supporters booed the Champions League anthem for years, they may enjoy its sound this season. They may not hear it again in the immediate future.

City started buying before they qualified for the Champions League – for Yaya Toure, David Silva and Carlos Tevez, their European debuts in sky blue came in lesser competitions – but for many a more recent arrival, it has provided part of the attraction.

And, while the sources of City’s income are a reason why they are imperilled, some of their revenue has come from the Champions League: more than £100m in 2022-23, when they won it. A club has been built with a financial model that entails expectations of competing at Europe’s top table.

“For sure, the Champions League for this organisation is so, so important,” said Maresca. It has formed part of their identity, especially during the long quest to win it. The last couple of seasons have marked a regression, with exits in the round of 24 and 16 respectively.

“We're going to try to improve compared to the last two, three years, where the team struggled a bit,” said Maresca. And if that scarcely feels the main issue confronting the club at the moment, it is the only one he can address. “We know how serious the situation is, but at the same time, it's not something that we can do. Where we can do things is inside the pitch,” said Maresca.
Their fate will be determined elsewhere. “We trust the club, we're very calm,” said Dias. “We have full confidence in the club. We will defend the club. We will fight for it.”

The bigger battle is not to stop Ousmane Dembele, Desire Doue and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. It is not to secure a top-eight finish in the league phase or even, given City’s 4-2 defeat in Paris in January 2025 that left them 25th, to avoid an ignominiously early exit.

There is the chance that, after 16 successive seasons in the Champions League, City’s time rubbing shoulders with the elite will reach an abrupt end. Because it is not merely in friendly banter that they are being branded cheats.
